Module 5

From C to a running program: compilers, linkers, executables and libraries

Modules 1 to 3 followed the two systems from power-on to a shell prompt. This module follows a program instead: a few lines of C, from the text file you type to the bytes a process executes. On MS-DOS 4.00 we use the toolchain that built MS-DOS itself, Microsoft C 5.10, MASM 5.10, LINK 3.65 and LIB 3.10, which ships in v4.0/src/TOOLS. On FreeBSD 15.1 we read the files produced by its own toolchain, clang and ld.lld, and the run-time linker /libexec/ld-elf.so.1. Each step (preprocess, compile, assemble, link, load) leaves a file or a memory image you can open, and the module opens every one of them: listings, object files, maps, executable headers, relocation tables and shared-library dependencies. Module 4 explains individual instructions; this module is about how instructions and data are packaged, combined and placed in memory.

MS-DOS 2d04cacFreeBSD release/15.1.018 source listings3 study cases7 exercisesabout 120 min read
Francesco Valerio Buccoli · francesco@buccoli.com

Learning goals. After this module you can:

  • name the stages from C source to a running process on both systems, the program that performs each stage and the file each stage produces;
  • run Microsoft C 5.10 pass by pass, read its .COD listing, and compare the code with x86-64 code for the same function;
  • explain the MS C memory models, near and far pointers and the segments _TEXT, _DATA, CONST, _BSS, DGROUP and STACK, and why 64-bit FreeBSD has code models but no memory models;
  • decode an OMF object file and an ELF relocatable object, and point to the symbol definitions, the external references and the relocations in each;
  • read a LINK map and an ELF symbol table, and trace the C start-up code from the entry point to main on both systems;
  • dump the header and relocation table of an MZ .EXE, state the rules that make a .COM file, and read the ELF header and program headers of an executable;
  • build and use a static library on both systems, and explain how FreeBSD's shared libraries are found, loaded and bound at run time (NEEDED, SONAME, PLT, GOT, ld-elf.so.1);
  • compare how MS-DOS EXEC and FreeBSD execve plus the run-time linker turn a file into a running program, including where relocation happens in each.

Prerequisites.

  • Module 0 (00-lab.md): the MS-DOS 4.00 image, tools/dos_run.py to run programs on it, and the FreeBSD 15.1 virtual machine. This module also uses tools/dos_tools.py, which runs the 1988 toolchain (read its docstring), nasm, and GNU readelf, objdump and nm on your own computer (any recent binutils that supports elf64-x86-64).
  • Module 2, section 2.6 (MS-DOS EXEC, FreeBSD execve and the image activator).
  • Module 4 (machine code and assembly language): registers, segment:offset addresses, the stack, CALL and RET.
  • C at the level of pointers, global variables and separate compilation.

5.1 The pipeline: from source text to a process#

A C program reaches the processor in five steps. Each step reads files and writes files, and the formats of those files are the subject of most of this module:

  1. Preprocessing expands #include and #define and removes comments. The result is still C text, called a translation unit.
  2. Compiling translates the translation unit into machine instructions for one processor and one calling convention.
  3. Assembling encodes the instructions as bytes and writes an object file: the bytes of code and data, the names the file defines, the names it needs from elsewhere, and a list of the places that cannot be completed until those names have addresses (relocations, called fixups in Microsoft's documentation).
  4. Linking combines object files and the needed parts of libraries into an executable file, deciding where every piece goes and patching the places the relocations point to.
  5. Loading copies or maps the executable into memory, finishes whatever the linker could not know (where the program actually landed), and jumps to the entry point. On FreeBSD a second linker, the run-time linker, runs at this point to attach shared libraries.
Stage MS-DOS 4.00 (Microsoft C 5.10) FreeBSD 15.1 (clang 19, LLD 19)
Driver CL.EXE cc (clang)
Preprocess pass 1 C1.EXE; CL /P writes .I, CL /E writes to standard output cc -E
Compile passes 1-3 C1, C2, C3; CL /Fa writes .ASM, /Fc a .COD listing cc -S writes .s
Assemble inside pass 3 C3.EXE: it writes the object file directly integrated assembler: cc -c
Object file .OBJ, Intel/Microsoft OMF .o, ELF relocatable (ET_REL)
Static library .LIB, made by LIB.EXE .a, made by ar
Link LINK.EXE 3.65, /MAP writes a map ld.lld, normally run by cc
Executable .COM (memory image) or .EXE (MZ header) ELF executable (ET_EXEC) or PIE (ET_DYN)
Shared library none .so, ELF ET_DYN with a SONAME
Load EXEC, INT 21h function 4Bh, in MSDOS.SYS execve(2) in the kernel, then ld-elf.so.1 in user mode

These are not just example tools: they are the tools each system was built with. The MS-DOS 4.00 tree compiles its C programs with the rule in Listing 5.1. The small memory model (-AS), optimization for size (-Os) and packed structures (-Zp) tell you that the authors counted bytes. FDISK, MEM, ATTRIB, REPLACE, FC, JOIN, SUBST and parts of BACKUP and RESTORE are C programs; the kernel, the BIOS and COMMAND.COM are assembly language.

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.1 – How the MS-DOS 4.00 build compiles C (TOOLS.INI lines 35-55)Source ↗
cc      =cl
cflags  =-AS -Os -Zp $(extcsw)
cinc    =-I. -I$(hinc)
⋮
.c.obj:
        $(cc) -c $(cflags) $(cinc) -Fo$*.obj $*.c

FreeBSD records its toolchain inside every binary, in the .comment section. The real /lib/libc.so.7 and /bin/ls from the 15.1 release say:

Output 5.1 – readelf -p .comment on FreeBSD 15.1's /bin/ls (real file from base.txz)
String dump of section '.comment':
  [     1]  Linker: LLD 19.1.7 (FreeBSD llvmorg-19.1.7-0-gcd708029e0b2-1500001) (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project.git llvmorg-19.1.7-0-gcd708029e0b2)
  [    8f]  FreeBSD clang version 19.1.7 (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project.git llvmorg-19.1.7-0-gcd708029e0b2)

The rest of this module uses one small program on both systems, HELLO.C (Example 5.1). It has a function, a call to a library function, an initialized global variable (data) and an uninitialized one (BSS), which is enough to exercise every part of the pipeline.

Example 5.1 – The program used throughout the module (labs/05-toolchain/HELLO.C; the FreeBSD copy labs/05-toolchain/freebsd/hello.c differs only in layout)
/* HELLO.C -- Module 5: one small C program for both toolchains */
#include <stdio.h>

int counter = 7;                /* initialized data */
int table[100];                 /* uninitialized data (BSS) */

int square(int x)
{
    return x * x;
}

int main(void)
{
    table[3] = square(counter);
    printf("hello, world: %d\n", table[3]);
    return 0;
}

5.2 Compiling: Microsoft C 5.10 and clang#

The CL driver and its three passes#

CL.EXE is a driver: it compiles nothing itself, it runs other programs. The TOOLS directory holds C1.EXE (114,521 bytes), C1L.EXE (149,303), C2.EXE (202,919) and C3.EXE (125,221) next to CL.EXE (31,329). The strings inside CL.EXE name c1.exe, c2.exe, c3.exe, link.exe, and options -B1, -B2, -B3 and -Bd. CL.HLP in the same directory, the text of CL /HELP, documents none of these. Trying them shows that /Bd makes CL print each pass's command line before running it, much like cc -v on FreeBSD:

Output 5.2 – CL /Bd /c HELLO.C, run with tools/dos_tools.py
---- CL /Bd /c HELLO.C
HELLO.C
P1 : ` T:\c1.exe -il 014595 -f HELLO.C -pc \:/ -ef T:\c1.err -Q 24242 -A snd -Ze -DM_I86 -DMSDOS -DM_I86SM -DM_I8086 -I T:/BLD/INC -W 1  '
P2 : ` T:\c2.exe -il 014595 -ef T:\c23.err -Oc -Ot -G0 -A snd -W 1  '
P3 : ` T:\c3.exe -il 014595 -ef T:\c23.err -T 0 -NM HELLO -FPi -Ot -c HELLO.OBJ -A snd -CC 0sO  '

Pass 1 (C1) is the front end: it preprocesses and parses, and it receives the predefined macros (M_I86, MSDOS, M_I86SM for the small model, M_I8086), the include path from INCLUDE, and a memory-model code, -A snd. With /AL (Lab 5.2) the code becomes -A lfd and the macro M_I86LM: the first letter is the code size (small or large), the second the default data pointer (near or far). -il 014595 is the base name of the intermediate files the passes hand to one another. Pass 2 (C2) optimizes and generates code (-Ot: optimize for time, the default; -G0: 8086 instructions). Pass 3 (C3) writes the object file HELLO.OBJ and, on request, the listings. There is no assembler pass: MASM is not involved when you compile C. /B1 T:\C1L.EXE replaces pass 1 by C1L.EXE, a larger build of the front end; with that option the same three lines appear with C1L.EXE in the first, and the object file is byte-for-byte identical.

Without /c, CL also writes a response file for the linker and runs it:

Output 5.3 – the link step that CL /Bd HELLO.C adds (excerpt)
HELLO.OBJ
HELLO.EXE /noi
NUL

;
LINK : ` link.exe @014628lk  '

Microsoft (R) Overlay Linker  Version 3.65
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1983-1988.  All rights reserved.

Object Modules [.OBJ]: HELLO.OBJ
Run File [HELLO.EXE]: HELLO.EXE /NOI
List File [NUL.MAP]: NUL
Libraries [.LIB]:

The four lines of the response file answer LINK's four prompts: object files, run file, list (map) file, libraries. The library line is empty, yet the program links against the C library. Section 5.4 shows where the library name is hidden.

Preprocessing#

CL /P HELLO.C writes the translation unit to HELLO.I (182 lines: the comments are gone, stdio.h is expanded). CL /E writes the same text to standard output with #line directives, so that the compiler can still report errors against the original file and line:

Output 5.4 – CL /E HELLO.C (beginning and end; blank lines in the middle removed)
#line 1 "HELLO.C"

#line 1 "T:/BLD/INC/stdio.h"
typedef unsigned int size_t;
#line 18 "T:/BLD/INC/stdio.h"
typedef char *va_list;
...
int cdecl printf(const char *, ...);
...
#line 3 "HELLO.C"

int counter = 7;
int table[100];
...

The prototypes carry the keyword cdecl, one of Microsoft's extensions (with near, far, huge and pascal) for 16-bit code: the C calling convention, in which the caller pushes the arguments from right to left and removes them afterwards. clang's equivalent is cc -E hello.c; it writes # 1 "hello.c" line markers instead of #line.

Reading the compiler's output: the .COD listing#

CL /c /Fc HELLO.C writes HELLO.COD: the source lines as comments, the assembly code the compiler generated, and the bytes and offsets of each instruction. It is the best way to see what a 1988 compiler did with your C.

Output 5.5 – HELLO.COD, the code part (real output of CL /c /Fc HELLO.C)
_TEXT      SEGMENT
        ASSUME  CS: _TEXT
;|*** int square(int x)
;|*** {
; Line 8
        PUBLIC  _square
_square PROC NEAR
        *** 000000      55                      push    bp
        *** 000001      8b ec                   mov     bp,sp
        *** 000003      33 c0                   xor     ax,ax
        *** 000005      e8 00 00                call    __chkstk
;       x = 4
;|***     return x * x;
; Line 9
        *** 000008      8b 46 04                mov     ax,WORD PTR [bp+4]      ;x
        *** 00000b      f7 e8                   imul    ax
        *** 00000d      5d                      pop     bp
        *** 00000e      c3                      ret
        *** 00000f      90                      nop

_square ENDP
;|*** int main(void)
;|*** {
; Line 13
        PUBLIC  _main
_main   PROC NEAR
        *** 000010      33 c0                   xor     ax,ax
        *** 000012      e8 00 00                call    __chkstk
;|***     table[3] = square(counter);
; Line 14
        *** 000015      ff 36 00 00             push    WORD PTR _counter
        *** 000019      e8 e4 ff                call    _square
        *** 00001c      83 c4 02                add     sp,2
        *** 00001f      a3 06 00                mov     WORD PTR _table+6,ax
;|***     printf("hello, world: %d\n", table[3]);
; Line 15
        *** 000022      50                      push    ax
        *** 000023      b8 02 00                mov     ax,OFFSET DGROUP:$SG163
        *** 000026      50                      push    ax
        *** 000027      e8 00 00                call    _printf
        *** 00002a      83 c4 04                add     sp,4
;|***     return 0;
; Line 16
        *** 00002d      2b c0                   sub     ax,ax
        *** 00002f      c3                      ret

Read it with Module 4 at hand:

  • Names get an underscore. square becomes _square, printf becomes _printf. This kept C names apart from assembly-language names in the same program.
  • Arguments are on the stack. main pushes counter, calls _square, and removes the argument with add sp,2; _square finds x at [bp+4], above the saved BP (2 bytes) and the near return address (2 bytes). The result comes back in AX. printf's two arguments are pushed right to left and removed with add sp,4.
  • Every function calls __chkstk with the size of its local variables in AX (here 0). It is the C library's stack-overflow check, and the reason why even main touches the library. /Gs (or /Ox) turns it off.
  • Unresolved bytes are zero. e8 00 00 (the call to _printf) and ff 36 00 00 (the address of counter) are incomplete; the object file will say how to complete them (section 5.4). The call to _square (e8 e4 ff) is already complete: it is relative to the next instruction, inside the same segment, so its displacement (-1Ch) does not depend on where the code is loaded.
  • table[3] is _table+6: the index is scaled by sizeof(int) = 2 at compile time.

The top of the same file declares the segments and the names:

Output 5.6 – HELLO.COD, the declarations (real output, abridged)
_TEXT   SEGMENT  WORD PUBLIC 'CODE'
_TEXT   ENDS
_DATA   SEGMENT  WORD PUBLIC 'DATA'
_DATA   ENDS
CONST   SEGMENT  WORD PUBLIC 'CONST'
CONST   ENDS
_BSS    SEGMENT  WORD PUBLIC 'BSS'
_BSS    ENDS
DGROUP  GROUP   CONST, _BSS, _DATA
        ASSUME  CS: _TEXT, DS: DGROUP, SS: DGROUP
PUBLIC  _counter
EXTRN   __acrtused:ABS
EXTRN   _printf:NEAR
EXTRN   __chkstk:NEAR
_BSS      SEGMENT
COMM NEAR       _table: BYTE:    200
_BSS      ENDS
_DATA      SEGMENT
        ORG     $+2
$SG163  DB      'hello, world: %d',  0aH,  00H
        ORG     $-20
_counter        DW      07H
_DATA      ENDS

counter is initialized, so it is in _DATA with its value 7. table is not: it is declared COMM, a communal variable of 200 bytes that the linker allocates (several modules may declare the same communal variable; the linker makes one). The string literal is in _DATA too, after counter: the ORG lines place it at offset 2. EXTRN __acrtused:ABS is a reference to a name that no code uses. Section 5.5 explains why it is there.

The same function from three compilers#

How much of this is the 8086 and how much is the 1988 compiler? FreeBSD's libc.so.7 contains abs(), whose source is one line (abs.c lines 34-38): return(j < 0 ? -j : j);. Here is the machine code clang 19 generated for it, disassembled from the real library, and what MS C 5.10 makes of the same line (in labs/05-toolchain, a function myabs with that body):

Output 5.7 – abs in FreeBSD 15.1's /lib/libc.so.7 (objdump -d --start-address=0x171970)
0000000000171970 <abs@@FBSD_1.0>:
  171970:       55                      push   %rbp
  171971:       48 89 e5                mov    %rsp,%rbp
  171974:       89 f8                   mov    %edi,%eax
  171976:       f7 d8                   neg    %eax
  171978:       0f 48 c7                cmovs  %edi,%eax
  17197b:       5d                      pop    %rbp
  17197c:       c3                      ret
Output 5.8 – myabs compiled by MS C 5.10 with CL /c /Ox /Fc (code part of the .COD)
        *** 000000      55                      push    bp
        *** 000001      8b ec                   mov     bp,sp
;|***     return(j < 0 ? -j : j);
        *** 000003      83 7e 04 00             cmp     WORD PTR [bp+4],0       ;j
        *** 000007      7d 07                   jge     $L20000
        *** 000009      8b 46 04                mov     ax,WORD PTR [bp+4]      ;j
        *** 00000c      f7 d8                   neg     ax
        *** 00000e      5d                      pop     bp
        *** 00000f      c3                      ret
        *** 000010      8b 46 04                mov     ax,WORD PTR [bp+4]      ;j
        *** 000013      5d                      pop     bp
        *** 000014      c3                      ret

Three differences stand out. The argument arrives in a register (%edi) on FreeBSD and on the stack ([bp+4]) on MS-DOS. clang avoids the branch with cmovs (conditional move if the sign flag is set); the 8086 has no conditional move (it appeared with the Pentium Pro), so MS C must branch. And /Ox removed the __chkstk call that the default options produce. Both functions still build a frame (push bp; mov bp,sp and push %rbp; mov %rsp,%rbp), although neither needs one.

Before Lab 5.8 gives you clang's output for HELLO.C itself (Output 5.41), any GCC can show x86-64 code for its functions. The output below comes from GCC 16 for Windows (MinGW-w64) on the course author's computer, run with -mabi=sysv so that it uses FreeBSD's calling convention (arguments in %rdi, %rsi, …). It is GCC, not FreeBSD's clang, so details differ.

Output 5.9 – gcc -S -O2 -mabi=sysv on square and the sum loop of Example 5.2 (directives removed)
square:
        imull   %edi, %edi
        movl    %edi, %eax
        ret
sum:
        testl   %esi, %esi
        jle     .L6
        movl    %esi, %esi
        xorl    %eax, %eax
        leaq    (%rdi,%rsi,4), %rdx
.L5:
        addl    (%rdi), %eax
        addq    $4, %rdi
        cmpq    %rdx, %rdi
        jne     .L5
        ret
.L6:
        xorl    %eax, %eax
        ret

At -O0 the same compiler stores x to the stack and reloads it, exactly like MS C's [bp+4] code; optimization is what moves values into registers.

MS C 5.10, small model FreeBSD amd64 (System V ABI)
int / pointer size 16 / 16 bits (32 for far pointers) 32 / 64 bits
Arguments on the stack, pushed right to left first six integer arguments in %rdi %rsi %rdx %rcx %r8 %r9
Return value AX (DX:AX for long and far pointers) %rax (%rdx:%rax for 128 bits)
Who removes arguments the caller (add sp,n) nothing to remove for register arguments
External names _square square
Stack check __chkstk on entry (off with /Gs) no call; an unmapped guard page below the stack (vm_map.c line 4637) and stack-protector canaries (__stack_chk_guard, section 5.7)

5.3 Memory models: segments versus a flat address space#

Why a C compiler for the 8086 needs memory models#

On the 8086 an address is a segment and a 16-bit offset (Module 4, section 4.2), so one segment register reaches at most 64 KB. A C pointer can therefore be a near pointer, 16 bits, an offset into a segment the compiler assumes is already in a register (DS for data, CS for code), or a far pointer, 32 bits, segment and offset, which must be loaded into a segment register before every use. Near pointers are small and fast but limit the program to 64 KB of data (or code); far pointers remove the limit and cost space and time. Microsoft C lets you choose per program with a memory model:

Option Model Code pointers, calls Data pointers Default library
/AS small (default) near: one _TEXT segment, at most 64 KB near: one DGROUP, at most 64 KB SLIBCE.LIB
/AM medium far: one segment per module near MLIBCE.LIB
/AC compact near far: data may exceed 64 KB CLIBCE.LIB
/AL large far far LLIBCE.LIB
/AH huge far far, and single arrays may exceed 64 KB

The four libraries are in v4.0/src/TOOLS/BLD/LIB; the E in the name stands for the floating-point emulator selected by the default /FPi (Output 5.2's -FPi). CL.HLP lists the five options. Whatever the model, DS and SS both point at DGROUP, the group of the segments _DATA (initialized data), CONST (constants), _BSS (uninitialized data) and STACK: that is what ASSUME CS: _TEXT, DS: DGROUP, SS: DGROUP in Output 5.6 says, and it is why a near pointer can point at a global variable or at a local variable on the stack without the compiler knowing which.

The same code in two models#

Example 5.2 – A function with a pointer argument, compiled in two models (labs/05-toolchain/MODELS.C)
/* MODELS.C -- Module 5: the same C code in two memory models */
#include <stdio.h>

int data[4] = { 1, 2, 3, 4 };

int sum(int *a, int n)
{
    int s = 0, i;

    for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
        s += a[i];
    return s;
}

int main(void)
{
    printf("sum = %d\n", sum(data, 4));
    return 0;
}

Compiled with /AS and /AL (Lab 5.2), the loop body and the call differ like this:

Output 5.10 – MODS.COD (/AS) and MODL.COD (/AL), the lines that differ (real output)
small model (/AS)                                large model (/AL)
_sum    PROC NEAR                                _sum    PROC FAR
  call  __chkstk          e8 00 00                 call  FAR PTR __chkstk  9a 00 00 00 00
;       a = 4                                    ;       a = 6
;       n = 6                                    ;       n = 10
  mov   si,WORD PTR [bp+4]  8b 76 04               les   si,DWORD PTR [bp+6]  c4 76 06
  mov   ax,[bx][si]         8b 00                  mov   ax,es:[bx][si]       26 8b 00
  ret                       c3                     ret                        cb
_main   PROC NEAR                                _main   PROC FAR
  mov   ax,OFFSET DGROUP:_data                     mov   ax,OFFSET DGROUP:_data
  push  ax                                         push  ds
                                                   push  ax
  call  _sum                e8 ba ff               push  cs
                                                   call  _sum                 e8 00 00
  add   sp,4                                       add   sp,6
  call  _printf             e8 00 00               call  FAR PTR _printf      9a 00 00 00 00

In the large model every function is FAR: it is called with a 5-byte CALL FAR (opcode 9A, offset and segment) and returns with RETF (CB), which pops a 4-byte return address, so the arguments move from [bp+4] to [bp+6]. The pointer a is 4 bytes, loaded with LES SI (offset into SI, segment into ES), and the access needs the ES: override prefix (26). The caller pushes DS to make data's address a far pointer. And one trick: _sum is in the same segment as _main, so the compiler fakes a far call with push cs followed by a 3-byte near call; RETF in _sum pops both. The code segment is named after the module, MODELS_TEXT, so that each module of a large program can have its own 64 KB.

The program grows from 7,301 to 10,033 bytes, and the number of segment relocations in the .EXE from 4 to 70 (Lab 5.2): every far call and every far address in the library holds a segment value that must be adjusted when the program is loaded.

FreeBSD: one flat address space, but code models#

A 64-bit FreeBSD process has one address space with 64-bit pointers (Module 2, section 2.1); there is no near or far, and long and pointers are both 64 bits wide. There are still code models in the x86-64 ABI, because most instructions carry at most a 32-bit displacement or immediate value. In the default small code model the compiler assumes that all code and static data of a program lie within 2 GB of each other, so it can address a global variable with a 32-bit displacement relative to the instruction pointer (%rip-relative addressing, as in mov 0x0(%rip),%eax). The large model drops that assumption and loads full 64-bit addresses with movabsq. FreeBSD's start-up code shows both forms:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.2 – Two ways to load the address of main (crt1_s.S lines 58-67)Source ↗
#ifdef PIC
        /*
         * XXX. %rip relative addressing is not intended for use in the
         * large memory model due to the offset from %rip being limited
         * to 32 bits.
         */
        leaq    main@plt(%rip), %r8
#else
        movabsq $main, %r8
#endif

The non-PIC branch is assembled into /usr/lib/crt1.o (Output 5.18 shows the movabs and its 64-bit relocation). The PIC branch is used for position-independent executables (PIE): programs linked as if loaded at address 0 and placed at a base address the kernel chooses at exec time, randomly if address space layout randomization is enabled (imgact_elf.c lines 1272-1293). Nearly everything in FreeBSD 15.1's /bin and /sbin is a PIE (Lab 5.7), because the base system's makefiles ask for it: they add -fPIE to the compiler flags and -pie to the linker flags (bsd.prog.mk lines 34-39), with the build option PIE on by default on 64-bit architectures (bsd.opts.mk lines 96-106). A plain cc hello.c does not: in the course VM it compiles with the static relocation model, links the non-PIC crt1.o and writes an ET_EXEC file linked at 0x200000 (Lab 5.8, Output 5.40). A PIE is the 64-bit cousin of an MZ .EXE: both are linked for address 0 and moved at load time; Study case 5.B compares how.

5.4 Object files: OMF and ELF#

An object file is the compiler's message to the linker. Whatever its format, it must say:

  1. the module's name and the translator that made it;
  2. the pieces of the module (segments or sections), with their sizes, alignment and how pieces of the same name from other modules are to be combined;
  3. the bytes of each piece;
  4. the names the module defines (public or global symbols) and where;
  5. the names it uses but does not define (external or undefined symbols);
  6. every place in the bytes that holds an address not yet known, and how to compute it (relocations).

Microsoft/Intel OMF#

MS-DOS object files use the Object Module Format (OMF) defined by Intel for the 8086 and extended by Microsoft. An OMF file is a sequence of records, each with a type byte, a 2-byte length, the contents and a checksum byte. labs/05-toolchain/omfdump.py decodes them; this is HELLO.OBJ, all 410 bytes:

Output 5.11 – python omfdump.py HELLO.OBJ (real output)

00000C  88 COMENT  class 00 (translator) 'MS C'
000016  88 COMENT  class 9F (default library) 'SLIBCE'
000022  88 COMENT  class 9D (memory model) '0sO'
00002B  88 COMENT  class A1 (debug info style) 01 43 56
000034  96 LNAMES  1='', 2='DGROUP', 3='_TEXT', 4='CODE', 5='_DATA', 6='DATA', 7='CONST', 8='_BSS', 9='BSS'

                    +028 offset16, self-relative: target EXT _printf; frame TARGET

                    +020 offset16, seg-relative: target EXT _table; frame TARGET

                    +013 offset16, self-relative: target EXT __chkstk; frame TARGET
                    +006 offset16, self-relative: target EXT __chkstk; frame TARGET
000195  8A MODEND  (no start address)
Record Says
THEADR (80h) module name
COMENT (88h) a comment with a class byte; several classes are instructions to the linker
LNAMES (96h) a list of names (segment, class and group names), numbered from 1
SEGDEF (98h) one segment: name and class (as LNAMES indexes), length, alignment, combine type
GRPDEF (9Ah) a group: segments that must fit in one 64 KB frame and are addressed from one segment value
EXTDEF (8Ch) names used here and defined elsewhere, numbered from 1
COMDEF (B0h) communal variables: uninitialized globals the linker allocates (numbered with the externals)
PUBDEF (90h) names defined here: segment and offset
LEDATA (A0h) bytes for a segment, starting at an offset
FIXUPP (9Ch) relocations for the preceding LEDATA, and threads (abbreviations used by later fixups)
MODEND (8Ah) end of module, with the program's start address if this is the main module

Three things in Output 5.11 deserve a closer look.

The library is named in the object file. COMENT class 9Fh says SLIBCE: "search this library by default". That is why CL left the library line of LINK's response file empty (Output 5.3) and why the /Zl option, "remove default library info" in CL.HLP, exists. Class 9Dh records the memory model.

Every fixup has a target and a frame. On the 8086 an address is relative to a segment value, so a fixup must say both what is addressed (the target: a segment, a group or an external name, plus a displacement) and relative to which segment base the 16-bit result is computed (the frame). Take push WORD PTR _counter at offset 15h, whose address field is at 17h. The target is segment _DATA (via thread T1) with displacement 0, the two bytes already in LEDATA, but the frame is the group DGROUP (thread F1). The linker must therefore store the distance from the start of DGROUP to _counter, not from the start of _DATA: at run time DS holds DGROUP's segment. In HELLO.MAP (Output 5.13) that distance is 42h. A self-relative fixup, like the one at 28h for call _printf, stores the distance from the end of the instruction to the target instead: that is what the E8 near call needs.

Not everything you see is needed. EXTDEF 4-6 declare _square and _main as externals although the same module defines them in PUBDEF; C1 declares every function it sees, and LINK accepts a definition in the same module. _square's call needs no fixup at all (Output 5.5). And __acrtused is external but no fixup refers to it: it exists only to make the linker pull in a library member (section 5.5).

ELF relocatable objects#

On FreeBSD the object file is an ELF file of type ET_REL. Instead of a stream of records it has a header and a table of sections, each a contiguous block: .text, .data, .bss, .rodata, the symbol table .symtab with its string table .strtab, and one relocation section per section that needs relocating (.rela.text for .text). Example 5.3 is a small x86-64 function in NASM syntax; Module 4 explains the instructions.

Example 5.3 – bump, which uses one variable and one function from other files (labs/05-toolchain/freebsd/bump.asm)
; bump.asm -- Module 5, Lab 5.6: a small x86-64 function as an ELF relocatable object
; Build:  nasm -f elf64 -o bump.o bump.asm
; C view: extern int counter; int step = 3;
;         void bump(void) { counter += step; report(counter); }
        default rel                     ; [name] means [rip + name]

        extern  counter                 ; an int defined in another object (main.c)
        extern  report                  ; a function defined in another object
        global  bump                    ; this object defines bump ...
        global  step                    ; ... and step for the others

        section .data
step:   dd      3

        section .text
bump:
        mov     eax, [counter]          ; counter is not in this file: relocation
        add     eax, [step]             ; step is, but .data has no address yet: relocation
        mov     [counter], eax
        mov     edi, eax                ; first integer argument in %edi (System V AMD64 ABI)
        jmp     report wrt ..plt        ; tail call through the PLT if report is in a library
Output 5.12 – readelf -s -r bump.o and objdump -d -r bump.o (real output, nasm -f elf64)

0000000000000002  0000000400000002 R_X86_64_PC32          0000000000000000 counter - 4
0000000000000008  0000000200000002 R_X86_64_PC32          0000000000000000 .data - 4
000000000000000e  0000000400000002 R_X86_64_PC32          0000000000000000 counter - 4
0000000000000015  0000000500000004 R_X86_64_PLT32         0000000000000000 report - 4

0000000000000000 <bump>:
   0:   8b 05 00 00 00 00       mov    0x0(%rip),%eax        # 6 <bump+0x6>
                        2: R_X86_64_PC32        counter-0x4
   6:   03 05 00 00 00 00       add    0x0(%rip),%eax        # c <bump+0xc>
                        8: R_X86_64_PC32        .data-0x4
   c:   89 05 00 00 00 00       mov    %eax,0x0(%rip)        # 12 <bump+0x12>
                        e: R_X86_64_PC32        counter-0x4
  12:   89 c7                   mov    %eax,%edi
  14:   e9 00 00 00 00          jmp    19 <bump+0x19>
                        15: R_X86_64_PLT32      report-0x4

Each relocation is an Elf64_Rela:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.3 – An ELF relocation entry (elf64.h lines 148-153)Source ↗
/* Relocations that need an addend field. */
typedef struct {
        Elf64_Addr      r_offset;       /* Location to be relocated. */
        Elf64_Xword     r_info;         /* Relocation type and symbol index. */
        Elf64_Sxword    r_addend;       /* Addend. */
} Elf64_Rela;

r_info packs a symbol index (high 32 bits) and a type (low 32 bits): 0000000400000002 is symbol 4, counter, type 2, R_X86_64_PC32 (elf_common.h lines 1675-1682). PC32 means "store symbol + addend - address of this field, as 32 bits". The addend is -4 because the processor adds the displacement to the address of the next instruction, which starts 4 bytes after the field. This is the same calculation as OMF's self-relative fixup; on x86-64 even data is addressed this way. The reference to step goes through the section symbol .data: the assembler knows step is at offset 0 of .data, but not where .data will be. R_X86_64_PLT32 asks the linker to reach report directly if it ends up in the same executable, or through a PLT entry if it is in a shared library (section 5.7).

OMF (.OBJ) ELF relocatable (.o)
Structure sequence of typed records header, section table, sections
Pieces segments (SEGDEF), groups (GRPDEF), classes sections, with flags (alloc, write, exec)
Defined names PUBDEF .symtab entries with a section index
Undefined names EXTDEF; uninitialized globals as COMDEF .symtab entries with UND; commons as SHN_COMMON
Relocations FIXUPP: location type, target, frame .rela.*: offset, symbol, type, addend
Address arithmetic 16-bit offsets relative to a frame, or segment values 32- or 64-bit, absolute or relative to %rip
Linker instructions COMENT records (default library, DOSSEG) .note and special sections; libraries named on the command line

5.5 Linking and the C run-time start-up#

What LINK does#

A linker reads all object files, then:

  1. collects segments: pieces with the same name and a public combine type are concatenated (all _TEXT pieces become one _TEXT), stack pieces are combined into one stack, and segments are ordered, normally by class;
  2. resolves names: every EXTDEF must meet a PUBDEF. Names still undefined after the object files are looked up in the libraries' dictionaries, and the library members that define them are added, which may bring new undefined names, until nothing changes. A name that no object file and no library defines is an error (Lab 5.5 shows L2029: Unresolved externals);
  3. assigns addresses to every segment and group and therefore to every public name;
  4. applies the fixups, writing final offsets into the bytes; and for every fixup that needs a segment value, which depends on where DOS will load the program, it adds an entry to the relocation table of the .EXE (section 5.6);
  5. writes the executable and, with /MAP, a map.
Output 5.13 – HELLO.MAP from LINK /MAP HELLO; (real output, abridged)

Program entry point at 0000:0040

The 48 bytes of HELLO.OBJ's code became a 5,889-byte (1701h) _TEXT: the rest is the C library. _counter is at 0171:0042, 42h bytes into DGROUP (which starts at paragraph 171h, linear 1710h), because the library's NULL segment comes first. That segment holds 8 zero bytes and the text MS Run-Time Library - Copyright (c) 1988, Microsoft Corp; when the program exits, the library routine __nullcheck XORs those 42h bytes and prints R6001 - null pointer assignment if the result has changed, which catches writes through near pointers that are 0. Likewise the first 16 bytes of _TEXT are zeros and _square starts at 0010h, so no C function has the address 0. table, the communal variable, landed in c_common. The stack is 800h = 2,048 bytes. And the program does not start at _main: the entry point is 0000:0040, __astart.

The start-up code: __astart and __acrtused#

Who defines __astart, and why is it linked at all? The library member that defines it also defines __acrtused, as an absolute symbol with the value 9876h. Every object file MS C writes contains an EXTDEF for __acrtused (Output 5.11): the reference makes LINK pull that member, the C run-time start-up, out of SLIBCE.LIB, and the value is irrelevant. omfdump.py --member shows the member:

This one member explains most of the map. It defines the STACK segment (800h bytes), its COMENT class 9Eh asks LINK for the DOSSEG segment order (code first, then DGROUP with initialized data before BSS and stack), and its MODEND carries the program's start address, _TEXT:0000, which is __astart. It is the only module with a start address, so it decides the entry point. And it is the one that calls _main (fixup at 8Eh). Disassembling its 178 bytes of code with ndisasm (the zeros are the places the fixups fill in) shows what happens between EXEC and main:

Matched against the fixups of Output 5.14, the start-up code:

  1. asks DOS for its version (AH=30h) and exits with INT 20h on DOS 1.x, which has no handle calls;
  2. loads DGROUP's segment (the fixup at 0Bh) and switches SS to it, so that SS = DS = DGROUP;
  3. gives back the memory it does not need with AH=4Ah (set block): EXEC gave the program as much as e_maxalloc asked for, often all free memory (Module 2, section 2.6);
  4. clears the BSS from _edata to _end with REP STOSB (fixups at 67h and 6Ah);
  5. calls __cinit (initializers), __setenvp and __setargv (build environ and argv from the PSP and the environment block);
  6. pushes environ, __argv and __argc and calls _main;
  7. pushes main's return value and calls _exit (C's exit). It runs the registered termination routines (one of them flushes the stdio buffers, or printf's output would be lost) and continues into __exit (C's _exit), which calls __nullcheck (and changes an exit code of 0 into 255 if the check failed), closes the handles 5-19 the program left open (function 3Eh) and ends with INT 21h function 4Ch.

FreeBSD: crt1.o, crti.o, crtbegin.o and __libc_start1#

FreeBSD's start-up code is split over several object files in /usr/lib, which cc adds to every link around your own objects and libraries: crt1.o, crti.o and crtbegin.o before them, crtend.o and crtn.o after them. These are the files a plain cc uses (Output 5.40 shows the exact command line, captured with cc -### in the course VM); cc -pie uses the PIC variants Scrt1.o, crtbeginS.o and crtendS.o, and cc -static uses crtbeginT.o. Their sources are in lib/csu ("C start-up").

Output 5.17 – nm on the start-up objects in FreeBSD 15.1's /usr/lib (real files)
-- crt1.o
0000000000000000 n .freebsd.noteG
                 U __libc_start1
0000000000000000 D __progname
0000000000000000 T _start
0000000000000000 B environ
                 U main
-- crti.o
0000000000000000 n .freebsd.noteG
0000000000000000 T _fini
0000000000000000 T _init
-- crtbegin.o
                 w .sizeof..dtors
                 w .startof..dtors
0000000000000000 d __CTOR_LIST__
0000000000000000 t __do_global_dtors_aux
0000000000000000 B __dso_handle
0000000000000000 d __DTOR_LIST__
-- crtend.o
                 w .startof..ctors
0000000000000000 d __CTOR_END__
0000000000000000 t __do_global_ctors_aux
0000000000000000 d __DTOR_END__
-- crtn.o

crt1.o plays the role of crt0: it defines the entry point _start and the variables environ and __progname, and it needs main and __libc_start1, exactly as crt0 defines __astart and needs _main. crti.o and crtn.o contribute the beginning and the end of the functions _init and _fini (crti.o has only push %rbp; mov %rsp,%rbp), and crtbegin.o/crtend.o bracket the lists of C++ constructors and destructors. _start itself is short:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.4 – The FreeBSD amd64 entry point (crt1_s.S lines 41-80)Source ↗
_start:
⋮
        pushq   %rbp                    /* Align stack, terminate call chain. */
⋮
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
⋮
        movq    %rsi, %rcx              /* cleanup */
        movslq  (%rdi), %rax            /* long *ap; tmpargc = *ap */
        leaq    0x8(%rdi), %rsi         /* argv = ap + 1 */
        leaq    0x10(%rdi, %rax, 8), %rdx /* env = ap + 2 + tmpargc */
        movl    %eax, %edi              /* argc = tmpargc */
⋮
        /* __libc_start1(argc, argv, env, cleanup, main) */
        callq   __libc_start1

The kernel (or the run-time linker) passes _start a pointer to the initial stack, where argc is followed by the argv pointers, a NULL, the environment pointers and another NULL; _start computes argv and env from it and hands everything, plus the address of main and a clean-up function from the run-time linker, to __libc_start1 in libc:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.5 – __libc_start1 calls main and passes its result to exit (libc_start1.c lines 159-181)Source ↗
void
__libc_start1(int argc, char *argv[], char *env[], void (*cleanup)(void),
    int (*mainX)(int, char *[], char *[]))
{
        handle_argv(argc, argv, env);

        if (&_DYNAMIC != NULL) {
                atexit(cleanup);
        } else {
                handle_irelocs(env);
                _init_tls();
        }

        handle_static_init(argc, argv, env);

        /*
         * C17 4.3 paragraph 3:
         * The value of errno in the initial thread is zero at program
         * startup.
         */
        errno = 0;
        exit(mainX(argc, argv, env));
}

&_DYNAMIC != NULL is how libc asks "am I in a dynamically linked program?": _DYNAMIC is a weak symbol that only the linker of a dynamic executable defines (libc_start1.c lines 44-45). In a dynamic program the run-time linker has already run the initializers, so libc only registers its clean-up function; in a static program libc must apply some relocations itself and run the initializers (handle_static_init, lines 97-123). handle_argv sets environ and __progname (lines 125-139). The two start-up paths do the same job: MS C's crt0 also sets up environ and argv and calls exit with main's value. What crt0 must do and crt1 need not: switch stacks, free memory, clear the BSS. On FreeBSD the kernel builds the stack and zero-fills BSS pages, and a process's memory is whatever its mappings say.

Output 5.18 – objdump -d -r /usr/lib/crt1.o (real file)
0000000000000000 <_start>:
   0:   55                      push   %rbp
   1:   48 89 e5                mov    %rsp,%rbp
   4:   48 89 f1                mov    %rsi,%rcx
   7:   48 63 07                movslq (%rdi),%rax
   a:   48 8d 77 08             lea    0x8(%rdi),%rsi
   e:   48 8d 54 c7 10          lea    0x10(%rdi,%rax,8),%rdx
  13:   89 c7                   mov    %eax,%edi
  15:   49 b8 00 00 00 00 00    movabs $0x0,%r8
  1c:   00 00 00
                        17: R_X86_64_64 main
  1f:   e8 00 00 00 00          call   24 <_start+0x24>
                        20: R_X86_64_PLT32      __libc_start1-0x4
  24:   cc                      int3

The 8-byte field at 17h gets the absolute address of main (R_X86_64_64), the call to __libc_start1 gets a PLT32 relocation like report in bump.o. In the FreeBSD 15.1 file set you can also see that cc does not link against libc.so.7 directly. /usr/lib/libc.so, the file the linker opens for -lc, is a 51-byte text file:

Output 5.19 – the contents of /usr/lib/libc.so in FreeBSD 15.1
GROUP ( /lib/libc.so.7 /usr/lib/libc_nonshared.a )

It is a linker script: link against the shared libc.so.7 and, for whatever that does not provide, the static libc_nonshared.a.

5.6 Executable files: .COM, MZ .EXE and ELF#

.COM: a memory image#

A .COM file has no header at all. EXEC decides that a file is a .COM when its first two bytes are not MZ (or ZM), whatever its name (Module 2, section 2.6). It allocates the largest free memory block, builds the 256-byte Program Segment Prefix (PSP) at its start, copies the whole file to offset 100h, sets CS = DS = ES = SS to the PSP's segment, and puts the stack at the top of the 64 KB segment:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.6 – Starting a .COM file (EXEC.ASM lines 593-612)Source ↗
        POP     SI                      ; get number of bytes to read
        jnc     OkRead
        jmp     exec_bad_file
OkRead:
        CMP     AX,SI                   ; did we read them all?
        JZ      exec_no_memj            ; exactly the wrong number... no memory
        TEST    BYTE PTR exec_func,exec_func_overlay
        JNZ     exec_set_PDB            ; no starto, chumo!
        MOV     AX,exec_DMA
        SUB     AX,10h
        MOV     exec_init_CS,AX
        MOV     exec_init_IP,100h       ; initial IP is 100
;
; SI is at most FF00h.  Add FE to account for PSP - word of 0 on stack.
;
        ADD     SI,0FEh                 ; make room for stack
        MOV     exec_init_SP,SI         ; max value for read is also SP!
        MOV     exec_init_SS,AX
        MOV     DS,AX
        MOV     WORD PTR [SI],0         ; 0 for return

SI is the number of bytes EXEC asked to read: FF00h when the block is at least 64 KB, which leaves room for the PSP (lines 573-580). If the read returns exactly that many bytes, EXEC cannot tell whether the file was longer, and it gives up with "not enough memory". So the largest .COM file MS-DOS 4.00 runs is FEFFh = 65,279 bytes, not 64 KB; Lab 5.4 checks this on the real system. The zero word pushed at the top of the stack lets a .COM program end with a plain RET, which jumps to offset 0 of the PSP, where an INT 20h instruction waits.

A .COM program has no relocations: it must work at whatever segment EXEC chooses, so it may contain offsets (all relative to the one segment) but never a segment value. MASM and LINK cannot write a .COM file directly. You write a program with ORG 100h in a single segment, link it into an .EXE, and convert it with EXE2BIN, whose rules (in MS-DOS 4.00's own EXE2BIN.EXE) are:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.7 – What EXE2BIN accepts (E2BINIT.ASM lines 746-789)Source ↗
        MOV     AX,[INITSS]
        OR      AX,[INITSP]
        OR      AX,[INITCS]
        JMP     ERRORNZ
⋮
xj:     MOV     AX,[INITIP]
        OR      AX,AX                   ;If IP=0, do binary fix
        JZ      BINFIX
        CMP     AX,100H                 ;COM file must be set up for CS:100
        JNZ     ERRORNZ
⋮
        SUB     [SIZ],AX                ;And count decreased size
        CMP     [RELCNT],0              ;Must have no fixups
        JNZ     ERRORNZ

The .EXE must have no stack segment and start at segment 0 (SS, SP and CS all zero). If IP is 100h the result is a .COM file: the first 100h bytes of the image (the space ORG 100h skipped) are dropped and there must be no relocations at all. If IP is 0 the result is a raw binary such as a device driver or a boot sector, and EXE2BIN asks "Fix-ups needed - base segment (hex):" if there are relocations. Anything else is "File cannot be converted". A C program fails the first test: crt0 brings a STACK segment, so SS:SP is not zero (Lab 5.4). The shell itself is built this way: COMMAND.COM is linked as COMMAND.EXE and converted by EXE2BIN (MAKEFILE lines 127-134), so its 32 object modules contain not a single segment fixup.

MZ .EXE: a header, a relocation table and an image#

The .EXE format starts with the two bytes MZ. The MS-DOS source declares the header as a structure, with a comment that names the author of the format:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.8 – The .EXE header (EXE.INC lines 52-71)Source ↗
EXE_file    STRUC
exe_signature   DW  ?                   ; must contain 4D5A  (yay zibo!)
exe_len_mod_512 DW  ?                   ; low 9 bits of length
exe_pages       DW  ?                   ; number of 512b pages in file
exe_rle_count   DW  ?                   ; count of reloc entries
exe_par_dir     DW  ?                   ; number of paragraphs before image
exe_min_BSS     DW  ?                   ; minimum number of para of BSS
exe_max_BSS     DW  ?                   ; max number of para of BSS
exe_SS          DW  ?                   ; stack of image
exe_SP          DW  ?                   ; SP of image
exe_chksum      DW  ?                   ; checksum  of file (ignored)
exe_IP          DW  ?                   ; IP of entry
exe_CS          DW  ?                   ; CS of entry
exe_rle_table   DW  ?                   ; byte offset of reloc table
exe_iov         DW  ?                   ; overlay number (0 for root)
exe_sym_tab     DD  ?                   ; offset of symbol table in file
EXE_file    ENDS

exe_valid_signature     EQU 5A4Dh
exe_valid_old_signature EQU 4D5Ah

"Zibo" is Mark Zbikowski, whose initials are the signature. labs/05-toolchain/mzdump.py prints these fields with both their EXE.INC names and the e_ names used in later documentation:

Output 5.20 – python mzdump.py HELLO.EXE (real output)
HELLO.EXE: 7271 bytes
  e_magic     exe_signature    0x5a4d  23117   signature 'MZ' (4D5Ah)
  e_cblp      exe_len_mod_512  0x0067    103   bytes used in the last 512-byte page
  e_cp        exe_pages        0x000f     15   number of 512-byte pages in the file
  e_crlc      exe_rle_count    0x0004      4   number of relocation entries
  e_cparhdr   exe_par_dir      0x0020     32   header size in 16-byte paragraphs
  e_minalloc  exe_min_BSS      0x00f0    240   extra paragraphs needed after the image
  e_maxalloc  exe_max_BSS      0xffff  65535   extra paragraphs wanted after the image
  e_ss        exe_SS           0x0216    534   initial SS, relative to the load segment
  e_sp        exe_SP           0x0800   2048   initial SP
  e_csum      exe_chksum       0x6b70  27504   checksum (ignored by MS-DOS)
  e_ip        exe_IP           0x0040     64   initial IP
  e_cs        exe_CS           0x0000      0   initial CS, relative to the load segment
  e_lfarlc    exe_rle_table    0x001e     30   file offset of the relocation table
  e_ovno      exe_iov          0x0000      0   overlay number (0 = main program)

  header + relocation table : 512 bytes
  load image                : 6759 bytes (423 paragraphs), file offsets 0x200-0x1c66
  memory needed             : image + 240 paragraphs = 663 paragraphs (10608 bytes), plus 16 paragraphs for the PSP
  entry point CS:IP         : 0000:0040 + load segment
  initial stack SS:SP       : 0216:0800 + load segment

  relocation table: 4 entries at file offset 0x1e
    entry  seg:off    image offset  word before loading
        0  0175:001E  0x00176e      0x0171
        1  0000:004B  0x00004b      0x0171
        2  0000:00D5  0x0000d5      0x0171
        3  0175:00B2  0x001802      0x0171

Everything here can be checked against the map (Output 5.13). The file is 14 full pages plus 103 bytes: 14 x 512 + 103 = 7,271. CS:IP = 0000:0040 is __astart. SS:SP = 0216:0800 is the end of the STACK segment, which starts at 2160h. The image is shorter than the program: _BSS, c_common and STACK hold no initialized bytes, so LINK leaves them out of the file and asks for them through e_minalloc (240 paragraphs). e_maxalloc = FFFFh asks for all the memory there is, which is why crt0 gives memory back with function 4Ah. And all four relocations point at words that contain 0171h, DGROUP's paragraph number in the image as linked. Two are operands in crt0's code (which starts at 40h): the mov di,0171h at 4Ah in __astart and the mov ax,0171h at D4h in __cintDIV, crt0's fixups at 0Bh and 95h in Output 5.14. The other two are words in the library's data. These are the only places in the program that hold a segment value. EXEC fixes them like this:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.9 – Relocating an .EXE: add the load segment to every listed word (EXEC.ASM lines 515-529)Source ↗
        MOV     SI,exec_rel_fac

exec_reloc_one:
        OR      DX,DX                   ; Any more entries?
        JE      exec_set_PDBJ

exec_get_addr:
        LDS     BX,DWORD PTR ES:[DI]    ; Get ra/sa of entry
        MOV     AX,DS                   ; Relocate address of item
        ADD     AX,SI
        MOV     DS,AX
        ADD     [BX],SI
        ADD     DI,4
        DEC     DX
        LOOP    exec_reloc_one          ; End of internal buffer?

exec_rel_fac is the segment where the image was loaded (PSP segment + 10h). Each table entry is a far pointer seg:off relative to the image; EXEC adds the load segment to the entry's segment to find the word, then adds the load segment to the word itself. After this, mov di,0171h has become mov di, the real paragraph of DGROUP. Two more details of EXEC are visible in real files:

  • The size in the header is trusted only roughly. EXEC computes the image size from e_cp alone, in whole pages (lines 314-319), and accepts a last read that comes up short by less than 512 bytes (lines 453-458). MS-DOS 4.00's own SORT.EXE depends on that: mzdump.py reports that the file ends 11 bytes before the end its header describes.
  • e_maxalloc = 0 means "load me high" (EXEC tests only this field, e_minalloc is then ignored): EXEC gives the program the largest free block and puts the image at the top of it instead of the bottom (lines 298-300, 370-371 and 394-398).

Several MS-DOS 4.00 programs, among them FIND.EXE, FDISK.EXE and EXE2BIN.EXE, have no relocations and an entry point at offset 10h of their last segment. They were linked with /EXEPACK (/E+ in FDISK.LNK line 1, /ex in FIND's MAKEFILE line 34): LINK compressed runs of repeated bytes and appended a small unpacker, marked by the bytes RB just before its entry point and by the message Packed file is corrupt. The unpacker expands the image in place, applies the relocations, which it keeps in its own packed table, with add [es:di],bx (the same addition as EXEC's ADD [BX],SI), and jumps to the real entry point. mzdump.py recognizes such files.

The .COM files of MS-DOS 4.00 hold a surprise of the same kind. Eight of them, among them FORMAT.COM, DEBUG.COM, CHKDSK.COM and BACKUP.COM, are built as .EXE files and then processed not by EXE2BIN but by a tool called CONVERT (for example FORMAT's MAKEFILE line 54 and BACKUP's line 44; only CONVERT.EXE itself is in TOOLS, without source). BACKUP is a C program with a stack segment and relocations, which EXE2BIN would refuse, yet the file is a .COM:

Output 5.21 – The start of BACKUP.COM from our build, and the code it jumps to (real bytes; ndisasm -o 0x100)
00000000: e9 9a 8f 43 6f 6e 76 65 72 74 65 64 00 00 00 00  ...Converted....
00000010: 4d 5a 85 01 48 00 3a 00 20 00 39 01 ff ff 91 09  MZ..H.:. .9.....

0000909D  E80000            call 0x90a0
000090A0  5B                pop bx
000090A1  50                push ax
000090A2  8CC0              mov ax,es
000090A4  051000            add ax,0x10
...
000090D9  26C5B51001        lds si,word [es:di+0x110]
...
000090EF  0104              add [si],ax
000090F1  E2E6              loop 0x90d9
...
00009102  F3A4              rep movsb
...
0000910D  FF6FF5            jmp word far [bx-0xb]

The file is a JMP to a stub at its end, the word Converted, and then the complete .EXE, MZ header included (58 relocations, e_crlc = 3Ah). EXEC loads it as a .COM. The stub computes the load segment (PSP + 10h), reads SS, SP, CS, IP and the relocation table from the embedded header, adds the load segment to every listed word with add [si],ax (the third copy of EXEC's relocation loop in this section), moves the image down to offset 100h with rep movsb, and jumps to the entry point. The program keeps the name and the loading rules of a .COM file and the structure of an .EXE.

ELF executables#

An ELF executable starts with the same 64-byte ELF header as an object file, but its type is ET_EXEC or ET_DYN, its entry point e_entry is filled in, and it has a program header table: the list of segments (an unfortunate name clash with x86 segments) that the kernel must map.

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.10 – A program header entry (elf64.h lines 115-124)Source ↗
typedef struct {
        Elf64_Word      p_type;         /* Entry type. */
        Elf64_Word      p_flags;        /* Access permission flags. */
        Elf64_Off       p_offset;       /* File offset of contents. */
        Elf64_Addr      p_vaddr;        /* Virtual address in memory image. */
        Elf64_Addr      p_paddr;        /* Physical address (not used). */
        Elf64_Xword     p_filesz;       /* Size of contents in file. */
        Elf64_Xword     p_memsz;        /* Size of contents in memory. */
        Elf64_Xword     p_align;        /* Alignment in memory and file. */
} Elf64_Phdr;
Output 5.22 – readelf -h -l bin/ls on FreeBSD 15.1's /bin/ls (real file, abridged)

  Segment Sections...
   01     .interp
   02     .interp .note.tag .dynsym .gnu.version .gnu.version_r .gnu.hash .hash .dynstr .rela.dyn .rela.plt .rodata .eh_frame_hdr .eh_frame
   03     .text .init .fini .plt
   04     .ctors .dtors .data.rel.ro .dynamic .got .relro_padding
   05     .data .got.plt .bss

Read it as the kernel does:

  • The byte 09 in the magic (e_ident[EI_OSABI]) is ELFOSABI_FREEBSD (elf_common.h line 171): the file is branded for FreeBSD.
  • DYN with an INTERP entry is a PIE. All addresses start near 0; the kernel adds a base address it chooses. The entry point 0x3ae0 is the start of .text, the PIC version of _start.
  • Four LOAD segments, each with its own permissions: read-only headers and constants, read-execute code, and two read-write parts. Where MemSiz exceeds FileSiz the kernel maps zero-filled memory for the rest: in the last one (0x4d1 versus 0x2c0) that is BSS, the ELF analogue of e_minalloc; in the third it is .relro_padding, which rounds the GNU_RELRO area up to a page boundary.
  • INTERP names the run-time linker, /libexec/ld-elf.so.1. DYNAMIC points at the table the run-time linker reads (section 5.7). GNU_RELRO marks data the run-time linker will make read-only after relocating it, and GNU_STACK with flags RW says the stack need not be executable.
  • Sections are for linkers and debuggers, segments for loaders. The mapping at the end shows which sections each segment contains. A loader never needs the section table; ls has 30 sections but the kernel looks only at the 11 program headers.

Only one ELF file in FreeBSD 15.1's /bin, /sbin and /libexec has no INTERP header (apart from the run-time linkers ld-elf.so.1 and ld-elf32.so.1 themselves): /sbin/init, 1,256,544 bytes, a static EXEC file linked at 0x200000. (A second static program is reachable from /sbin: /sbin/nologin is a symbolic link to /usr/sbin/nologin, which is linked statically too, so that LD_LIBRARY_PATH cannot make a disabled account's login shell load another libc (usr.sbin/nologin/Makefile lines 6-11); Exercise 5.6 finds it.) The makefile of init asks for static linking with NO_SHARED?= YES (Makefile line 13), so the first process (Module 1, section 1.4) runs even if a shared library is missing or damaged:

Output 5.23 – readelf -h -l sbin/init (real file, abridged)

  Entry point address:               0x241410
...

  LOAD           0x000000000012d820 0x000000000032f820 0x000000000032f820
  LOAD           0x000000000012e2b0 0x00000000003312b0 0x00000000003312b0
  TLS            0x000000000012d820 0x000000000032f820 0x000000000032f820
.COM MZ .EXE ELF executable

Recognized by absence of MZ MZ (or ZM) \x7fELF, class, OS/ABI brand
