5.7 Libraries: static everywhere, shared only on FreeBSD#

Static libraries on MS-DOS: .LIB#

A .LIB file is a collection of OMF modules, each starting on a page boundary, followed by a dictionary that maps every public name to the module that defines it. LIB.EXE builds and edits libraries (+ adds a module, - removes one, -+ replaces, * extracts) and writes a listing. omfdump.py --modules lists the members; the C library of the small model has 402 of them:

Output 5.24 – python omfdump.py SLIBCE.LIB --modules (real output, abridged)
000010  dos\crt0.asm    190 bytes  __aexit_rtn __abrkp __abrktb __asizds __astart __atopsp __abrktbe __cintDIV __acrtused __amsg_exit
000370  dos\crt0dat.asm    429 bytes  __osversion _errno __exit __child __nfile __cinit ___argc __intno ...
000A10  dos\crt0msg.asm    166 bytes  __FF_MSGBANNER __adbgmsg __acrtmsg
000BF0  crt0fp.asm       47 bytes  __fptrap
000D10  chkstk.asm       24 bytes  STKHQQ __chkstk
...
002E00  printf.c         60 bytes  _printf
...
006660  write.asm       296 bytes  _write
...
00B4E0  puts.c          106 bytes  _puts

The module names are the original source file names: the library was written partly in C and partly in assembly, with the MS-DOS-specific parts in a dos directory. LINK adds a member only when it defines a name that is still undefined, and it adds the whole member: that is why library authors put one function (or a few that are always used together) in each module. printf.c is 60 bytes because it only calls the real formatter: its EXTDEF record names __output, which lives in another member. puts.c needs _fwrite and _strlen but not __output, so a program that prints with puts alone does not carry the formatter. Lab 5.5 builds a two-member library and shows in the map that an unused member is left out.

What MS-DOS had instead of shared libraries#

MS-DOS 4.00 has no shared libraries. Every C program carries its own copy of the parts of the library it uses: HELLO.EXE is 7,271 bytes for a 48-byte main, and MS-DOS's own MEM.EXE (20,005 bytes), linked from MEM.C with the same library, has the same NULL, _DATA, c_common and 2 KB STACK segments in its map as HELLO.EXE. The only code shared by all programs is the operating system itself, reached through interrupt vectors: a program calls printf's output routine in its own image, which calls _write, which executes INT 21h function 40h. An interrupt number is a binding by number rather than by name, resolved at run time through the interrupt vector table, which any program can change (Module 2, section 2.1). Study case 5.C follows that thought to resident programs and INT 2Fh.

FreeBSD static libraries: .a#

On FreeBSD a static library is an ar archive of ELF objects with a symbol index. The base system ships /usr/lib/libc.a (1,432 members) and /usr/lib/libsys.a (464 members) for static linking (cc -static, and programs such as /sbin/init). The rules are the same as LINK's: members are added whole, only to satisfy undefined names.

Output 5.25 – ar t libc.a (selected members) and nm of printf.o in it (real files)
libc_start1.o
printf.o
vfprintf.o
write.o
abs.o

usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:                 U __stack_chk_fail
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:                 U __stack_chk_guard
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:                 U __stdoutp
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:0000000000000000 T printf
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:00000000000000c0 T printf_l
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:                 U vfprintf
usr/lib/libc.a:printf.o:                 U vfprintf_l

As in MS C's library, printf is a thin wrapper (it needs vfprintf); the two __stack_chk names are the stack protector, a canary value checked before a function returns.

Shared libraries: SONAME and NEEDED#

A shared library is linked once into an ELF file of type ET_DYN and attached to programs when they run, so that one copy on disk, and in memory, serves every process. The program records only the library's name. readelf -d shows the dynamic section (PT_DYNAMIC), a table of tag-value pairs that is the run-time linker's input:

Output 5.26 – readelf -d on /bin/ls, /lib/libc.so.7 and /lib/libsys.so.7 (real files, abridged)
/bin/ls: Dynamic section at offset 0x7a60 contains 25 entries:
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libutil.so.10]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libtinfow.so.9]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libc.so.7]
 0x000000006ffffffb (FLAGS_1)            Flags: PIE
 0x0000000000000007 (RELA)               0x1350
 0x0000000000000017 (JMPREL)             0x14d0
 0x0000000000000002 (PLTRELSZ)           1824 (bytes)
 0x0000000000000003 (PLTGOT)             0xaca8
 0x0000000000000006 (SYMTAB)             0x308
 0x0000000000000005 (STRTAB)             0xfb4

/lib/libc.so.7: Dynamic section at offset 0x1f33d0 contains 30 entries:
 0x000000007ffffffd (AUXILIARY)          Auxiliary library: [libsys.so.7]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libsys.so.7]
 0x000000000000000e (SONAME)             Library soname: [libc.so.7]

/lib/libsys.so.7: Dynamic section at offset 0x1a640 contains 22 entries:
 0x000000000000000e (SONAME)             Library soname: [libsys.so.7]
 0x000000000000001e (FLAGS)              SYMBOLIC

SONAME is the name a library gives itself; the linker copies it into the NEEDED entries of every program linked against it. The 7 is the major version, set in the library's makefile (SHLIB_MAJOR= 7, libc/Makefile line 32): it changes only when old programs could no longer work with the new library. Within a major version, FreeBSD keeps old interfaces alive with symbol versions: the dynamic symbol table lists printf@@FBSD_1.0, __libc_start1@@FBSD_1.7, and a program records which version of each symbol it was linked against.

FreeBSD 15: system calls in libsys#

Before FreeBSD 15, libc contained the system call stubs. In FreeBSD 15 the shared libc keeps only empty placeholders for them (sys/Makefile.inc lines 8-9; the static libc.a still has the real ones): they live in a separate library, libsys.so.7, which libc needs (Output 5.26). libc's makefile links it in and declares libc an auxiliary filter of libsys:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.11 – libc needs libsys (libc/Makefile lines 64-73)Source ↗
LDFLAGS+= -nodefaultlibs
LIBADD+=        compiler_rt
LIBADD+=        sys
⋮
LDFLAGS+=-Wl,--auxiliary,libsys.so.7

An auxiliary filter means: when a symbol is found in libc, the run-time linker also looks for it in libsys and prefers libsys's definition if there is one; otherwise libc's own definition stands (rtld.c lines 4990-5008). rtld(1) adds that filtees are normally opened at the first lookup through the filter. The C function write remains in libc, as a call through a table of interposing slots, so that the threading library can replace system calls that must cooperate with threads (Makefile.sys lines 15-18):

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.12 – libc's write (write.c lines 37-42)Source ↗
#pragma weak write
ssize_t
write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t nbytes)
{
        return (INTERPOS_SYS(write, fd, buf, nbytes));
}

libsys's table maps the slot to __sys_write (interposing_table.c line 67), and __sys_write is the actual system call stub, generated from the PSEUDO macro in SYS.h (Makefile.sys lines 158-162; Module 4, Lab 4.7 reads it instruction by instruction). In the real binaries:

Output 5.27 – write in libc and __sys_write in libsys (readelf --dyn-syms, objdump -d; real files)
libc.so.7:   3097: 0000000000144f00    53 FUNC    WEAK   DEFAULT   14 write@@FBSD_1.0
libc.so.7:   1818: 0000000000128aa0   188 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT   14 printf@@FBSD_1.0
libsys.so.7:  853: 000000000001b4a0    17 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT   13 __sys_write@@FBSDprivate_1.0
libsys.so.7:  751: 000000000001b4a0    17 FUNC    WEAK   DEFAULT   13 _write@@FBSDprivate_1.0

000000000001b4a0 <__sys_write@@FBSDprivate_1.0>:
   1b4a0:       b8 04 00 00 00          mov    $0x4,%eax
   1b4a5:       49 89 ca                mov    %rcx,%r10
   1b4a8:       0f 05                   syscall
   1b4aa:       0f 82 58 c9 ff ff       jb     17e08 <__sys_vfork@@FBSDprivate_1.0+0x18>
   1b4b0:       c3                      ret

Seventeen bytes: system call number 4 in %eax, the syscall instruction, and a jump to the error handler cerror if the carry flag reports an error (Module 2, section 2.2.5). objdump names the target after the nearest symbol it knows, __sys_vfork; the jump really goes to the local cerror code. The MS-DOS counterpart, the library's _write in write.asm, issues INT 21h with AH=40h (visible with ndisasm in the member's code).

Lazy binding: PLT and GOT#

A call from ls to getenv in libc cannot be a direct call with a fixed displacement: neither ls's nor libc's address is known until run time, and the code pages must stay read-only so that all processes can share them. The linker therefore routes each call through two small tables: the procedure linkage table (PLT, code, read-only) and the global offset table (GOT, data, writable). The call goes to a PLT entry, which jumps through a GOT slot:

Output 5.28 – PLT entries and the initial GOT of FreeBSD 15.1's /bin/ls (objdump; real file)
    4067:       e8 f4 44 00 00          call   8560 <getenv@plt>

00000000000084f0 <__libc_start1@plt-0x10>:
    84f0:       ff 35 ba 27 00 00       push   0x27ba(%rip)        # acb0 <__progname@@Base+0x50>
    84f6:       ff 25 bc 27 00 00       jmp    *0x27bc(%rip)        # acb8 <__progname@@Base+0x58>
    84fc:       0f 1f 40 00             nopl   0x0(%rax)

0000000000008500 <__libc_start1@plt>:
    8500:       ff 25 ba 27 00 00       jmp    *0x27ba(%rip)        # acc0 <__libc_start1@FBSD_1.7>
    8506:       68 00 00 00 00          push   $0x0
    850b:       e9 e0 ff ff ff          jmp    84f0 <_fini@@Base+0x18>

Contents of section .got.plt:
 aca8 609a0000 00000000 00000000 00000000  `...............
 acb8 00000000 00000000 06850000 00000000  ................
 acc8 16850000 00000000 26850000 00000000  ........&.......

In the file, the GOT slot for __libc_start1 (at 0xacc0) contains 0x8506: the address of the push instruction in its own PLT entry. The first call therefore jumps through the slot right back into the PLT, pushes the index of the relocation (0), and jumps to the common entry PLT0, which pushes GOT[1] and jumps through GOT[2]. Those two slots are 0 in the file (GOT[0], 0x9a60, is the address of _DYNAMIC); the run-time linker fills them before the program runs:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.13 – The two GOT slots the PLT needs (reloc.c lines 120-128)Source ↗
/* Initialize the special GOT entries. */
void
init_pltgot(Obj_Entry *obj)
{
        if (obj->pltgot != NULL) {
                obj->pltgot[1] = (Elf_Addr)obj;
                obj->pltgot[2] = (Elf_Addr)&_rtld_bind_start;
        }
}

_rtld_bind_start saves the registers and calls _rtld_bind, which finds the relocation by its index, looks the symbol up in the loaded objects and writes the address into the GOT slot:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.14 – Binding one PLT slot on first use (rtld.c lines 1056-1104)Source ↗
Elf_Addr
_rtld_bind(Obj_Entry *obj, Elf_Size reloff)
{
⋮
        where = (Elf_Addr *)(obj->relocbase + rel->r_offset);
        def = find_symdef(ELF_R_SYM(rel->r_info), obj, &defobj, SYMLOOK_IN_PLT,
            NULL, &lockstate);
        if (def == NULL)
                rtld_die();
⋮
        target = reloc_jmpslot(where, target, defobj, obj, rel);
        lock_release(rtld_bind_lock, &lockstate);
        return (target);
}

reloc_jmpslot simply stores the target in the slot (reloc.c lines 414-423), and _rtld_bind_start jumps to the function. From the second call on, the PLT's first jmp goes straight to libc. This is lazy binding: a program that calls 76 library functions (the 76 JUMP_SLOT relocations of ls) pays for the lookup of only those it actually calls. Setting LD_BIND_NOW makes the run-time linker bind every slot before the program starts, which, in rtld(1)'s words, "avoids run-time surprises caused by unexpectedly undefined functions". Data references cannot be lazy: the 16 entries of ls's .rela.dyn (six R_X86_64_RELATIVE, nine R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT, for example for __stdoutp and __stack_chk_guard, and one thread-local R_X86_64_TPOFF64) are all applied at start-up (section 5.8).

Where does the run-time linker look for libc.so.7? rtld(1) gives the order: the program's DT_RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, the program's DT_RUNPATH, the hints file built by ldconfig(8), then /lib and /usr/lib. LD_LIBRARY_PATH, LD_PRELOAD and the other LD_ variables that choose what gets loaded are ignored for set-user-ID programs, so a user cannot make su load a library of their choice. And ldd(1) is not a separate parser of ELF files: it sets LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS (ldd.c lines 198-207) and runs the program through the run-time linker, which loads the libraries, prints them and exits before main (Lab 5.8).

5.8 Loading: EXEC versus execve and the run-time linker#

MS-DOS: everything inside one INT 21h call#

Module 2 (section 2.6) traced EXEC, INT 21h function 4Bh, step by step. Seen from the file formats of this module, it does four things, all inside the kernel and before the program's first instruction:

  1. it reads the first 1Ah bytes and decides between .COM and .EXE by the signature;
  2. it allocates a memory block (the largest one for a .COM, image plus e_minalloc to e_maxalloc paragraphs for an .EXE) and builds the PSP at its start;
  3. it reads the image, in chunks of at most FE00h bytes, and for an .EXE adds the load segment to every word in the relocation table (Listing 5.9) and to CS and SS (EXEC.ASM lines 470-483);
  4. it loads SS:SP, sets DS = ES = PSP and jumps to CS:IP (Module 2, Listing 2.24).

There is no name lookup anywhere: by the time EXEC runs, LINK has resolved every name, and the file contains only numbers. The program's own start-up code (__astart, Output 5.15) then does the rest.

FreeBSD: execve, then the run-time linker#

execve (Module 2, section 2.6) offers the file to each image activator in turn; the ELF activator, exec_elf64_imgact in imgact_elf.c, accepts ET_EXEC and ET_DYN files. It walks the program headers, records the PT_LOAD segments and reads the PT_INTERP path (lines 1174-1215), chooses a base address for a PIE (lines 1272-1293), replaces the address space and maps every PT_LOAD segment (lines 743-762). Then comes the step that has no MS-DOS counterpart:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.15 – The entry point becomes the run-time linker's (imgact_elf.c lines 1384-1406)Source ↗
        entry = (u_long)hdr->e_entry + imgp->et_dyn_addr;
        imgp->entry_addr = entry;

        if (sv->sv_protect != NULL)
                sv->sv_protect(imgp, SVP_IMAGE);

        if (interp != NULL) {
                VOP_UNLOCK(imgp->vp);
                if ((map->flags & MAP_ASLR) != 0) {
                        /* Assume that interpreter fits into 1/4 of AS */
                        maxv1 = maxv / 2 + addr / 2;
                        error = __CONCAT(rnd_, __elfN(base))(map, addr,
                            maxv1, PAGE_SIZE, &addr);
                }
                if (error == 0) {
                        error = __elfN(load_interp)(imgp, brand_info, interp,
                            &addr, &imgp->entry_addr);
                }
                vn_lock(imgp->vp, LK_SHARED | LK_RETRY);
                if (error != 0)
                        goto ret;
        } else
                addr = imgp->et_dyn_addr;

The program's entry point (e_entry plus the PIE base) is computed and kept in entry. If there is an interpreter, load_interp maps /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 too, itself an ET_DYN file with its own LOAD segments and no INTERP, and overwrites imgp->entry_addr with its entry point. The kernel will start the process in the run-time linker. It tells the run-time linker where things are through the auxiliary vector, an array of type-value pairs placed on the new stack after the environment: AT_PHDR (where the program's headers are mapped), AT_ENTRY (the program's own entry point, entry above) and AT_BASE (where the interpreter was loaded) (lines 1464-1470). For a static program like /sbin/init there is no interpreter and the process starts at the program's own _start.

The run-time linker's entry point is a few lines of assembly that call the C function _rtld and jump to whatever address it returns:

FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.16 – ld-elf.so.1 starts here (rtld_start.S lines 30-51)Source ↗
.rtld_start:
        .cfi_startproc
        .cfi_undefined %rip
        xorq    %rbp,%rbp               # Clear frame pointer for good form
        subq    $24,%rsp                # A place to store exit procedure addr
        .cfi_def_cfa_offset 32
        movq    %rdi,%r12
        movq    %rsp,%rsi               # save address of exit proc
        movq    %rsp,%rdx               # construct address of obj_main
        addq    $8,%rdx
        call    _rtld                   # Call rtld(sp); returns entry point
        popq    %rsi                    # Get exit procedure address
        .cfi_def_cfa_offset 24
        movq    %r12,%rdi               # *ap
/*
 * At this point, %rax contains the entry point of the main program, and
 * %rdx contains a pointer to a termination function that should be
 * registered with atexit().  (crt1.o registers it.)
 */
.globl .rtld_goto_main
.rtld_goto_main:        # This symbol exists just to make debugging easier.
        jmp     *%rax                   # Enter main program

_rtld (rtld.c lines 532-1043) is the run-time linker's main. In order, it:

  1. finds argc, argv, the environment and the auxiliary vector on the stack, and relocates itself, since it is a PIE-like shared object loaded at AT_BASE and "has not been relocated yet" (lines 551-579);
  2. reads the LD_ environment variables, dropping the unsafe ones (LD_LIBRARY_PATH, LD_PRELOAD, …) if the program is set-user-ID or set-group-ID (lines 732-767);
  3. builds a descriptor for the program from AT_PHDR and AT_ENTRY and reads its dynamic section (lines 791-842);
  4. maps the kernel's vDSO and any LD_PRELOAD libraries, then every NEEDED library, recursively, in breadth-first order (load_needed_objects), and exits right there if LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS is set:
FreeBSD 15.1Listing 5.17 – Loading the needed libraries, or only listing them for ldd (rtld.c lines 884-913)Source ↗
        dbg("loading needed objects");
        if (load_needed_objects(obj_main,
                ld_tracing != NULL ? RTLD_LO_TRACE : 0) == -1)
                rtld_die();
⋮
        if (ld_tracing) { /* We're done */
                trace_loaded_objects(obj_main, true);
                exit(0);
        }
  1. applies the relocations of every object (relocate_objects, lines 947-950): R_X86_64_RELATIVE adds the object's base address, *where = relocbase + addend (reloc.c lines 310-312), R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT looks a symbol up, and the PLT slots are prepared for lazy binding, or bound now if LD_BIND_NOW is set;
  2. runs the initialization functions of the libraries and of the program itself, which FreeBSD's crt1.o leaves to the run-time linker (objlist_call_init, line 1019), makes the GNU_RELRO area read-only (lines 1030-1032) and returns the program's entry point (lines 1036-1042).

.rtld_goto_main then jumps to the program's _start (Listing 5.4). The address of the run-time linker's exit procedure, which _rtld stored on the stack, is popped into %rsi: that is _start's second argument, cleanup, which __libc_start1 registers with atexit. (The comment in Listing 5.16 says %rdx; the code and crt1_s.S agree on %rsi. Read the code, not only the comments.)

MS-DOS 4.00 EXEC FreeBSD 15.1 execve + ld-elf.so.1
Who loads the kernel, entirely the kernel maps the program and the interpreter; the interpreter maps the libraries
How read into a memory block mmap of file pages, read on demand
What is relocated segment values listed in the header addresses in data and GOT, per relocation type
Names at load time none dynamic symbol tables, looked up by hash
When code is bound at link time at start-up (data) and at first call (functions)
Where relocation runs in the kernel (MSDOS.SYS) in user mode, in the new process
Failure modes "Program too big to fit in memory", "Error in EXE file" (COMMAND1.ASM lines 423-431) ENOEXEC, "ELF interpreter … not found", or Shared object "..." not found, required by "..." (rtld.c line 1998)

Labs#

All MS-DOS labs use a working copy of labs/05-toolchain, for example work\05, and the course tools from the repository root. dos_tools.py runs the 1988 toolchain in DOSBox-X's own DOS with your directory as drive D:; dos_run.py runs the result on the MS-DOS 4.00 we built. The ELF labs need GNU readelf, objdump and nm, and the FreeBSD 15.1 files from base.txz (the course keeps them in build/freebsd/root; in the FreeBSD VM use / instead, and expect LLVM's versions of the three tools, which print the same facts in a slightly different layout: Lab 5.7, Output 5.39).

Lab 5.1: HELLO.C with Microsoft C 5.10, one pass at a time#

Goal. Produce and read every intermediate file of the MS-DOS pipeline, and run the result.

What you need. HELLO.C (Example 5.1), tools/dos_tools.py, tools/dos_run.py.

Steps.

  1. Preprocess, compile with a listing, and link with a map:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work/05 "CL /P HELLO.C" "CL /c /Fc HELLO.C" "LINK /MAP HELLO;" "DIR"

  2. Open HELLO.I, HELLO.COD and HELLO.MAP in an editor.

  3. Repeat the compile step with CL /Bd /c HELLO.C to see the three passes (Output 5.2).

  4. Run the program on MS-DOS 4.00:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\HELLO.EXE=work/05/HELLO.EXE "HELLO" "DIR HELLO.EXE"

What you should see.

Output 5.29 – Lab 5.1, step 1 (real output; the dates are DOSBox-X's)
---- CL /P HELLO.C
---- CL /c /Fc HELLO.C
HELLO.C
---- LINK /MAP HELLO;

Microsoft (R) Overlay Linker  Version 3.65
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1983-1988.  All rights reserved.

---- DIR
...
HELLO    C                  371 11/09/2026  9:40a
HELLO    COD              2,050 11/09/2026  8:40a
HELLO    EXE              7,271 11/09/2026  8:40a
HELLO    I                2,646 11/09/2026  8:40a
HELLO    MAP              7,566 11/09/2026  8:40a
HELLO    OBJ                410 11/09/2026  8:40a

The listing is Output 5.5 and 5.6, the map Output 5.13, the run Output 5.16 (hello, world: 49).

What is going on. CL /P stops after pass 1; CL /c runs the three passes and writes the object file directly (section 5.2); LINK finds SLIBCE.LIB through the COMENT record in HELLO.OBJ and starts the program at __astart from crt0 (section 5.5). HELLO.I has 182 lines for a 17-line program because stdio.h is expanded in place; the comments and the directives are gone, leaving blank lines.

Questions.

  1. List the bytes in HELLO.COD that are still 00 and say, for each, what will fill them in and when.
  2. HELLO.OBJ holds 48 bytes of code and 20 of data, HELLO.EXE is 7,271 bytes. Use the map to find which library routines account for most of the difference.
  3. Change int counter = 7; to int counter;. Predict how counter appears in the .COD, in the object file and in the map, then check.

Lab 5.2: Memory models in the generated code#

Goal. See near and far pointers and calls in real compiler output, and measure their cost.

What you need. MODELS.C (Example 5.2).

Steps.

  1. Compile and link the same file in the small and the large model, keeping both listings:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work/05 "CL /AS /FcMODS.COD /FoMODS.OBJ /FeMODS.EXE MODELS.C" "CL /Bd /AL /FcMODL.COD /FoMODL.OBJ /FeMODL.EXE MODELS.C"

  2. Compare the listings (fc MODS.COD MODL.COD on Windows, diff elsewhere) and the pass command lines of the /AL compile with Output 5.2.

  3. Run both programs and compare their sizes:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_run.py --file A:\MODS.EXE=work/05/MODS.EXE --file A:\MODL.EXE=work/05/MODL.EXE "MODS" "MODL" "DIR MOD?.EXE"

  4. Count the relocations: python labs/05-toolchain/mzdump.py work/05/MODS.EXE --quiet and the same for MODL.EXE.

What you should see. The differences are those of Output 5.10. The /AL passes are called with -A lfd and -DM_I86LM instead of -A snd and -DM_I86SM. Both programs print the same result:

Output 5.30 – Lab 5.2, step 3 (real output)
---- MODS
sum = 10
---- MODL
sum = 10
---- DIR MOD?.EXE

 Volume in drive A is DOS400LAB
 Volume Serial Number is 1988-0400
 Directory of  A:\

MODS     EXE      7301 04-25-24  12:00p
MODL     EXE     10033 04-25-24  12:00p
        2 File(s)     259072 bytes free

mzdump.py reports e_crlc = 4 for MODS.EXE and 70 for MODL.EXE, and the large model's entry point is 0006:0012 instead of 0000:0068: the code no longer starts with the library's _TEXT but with MODELS_TEXT.

What is going on. A far call names a segment, and a segment value depends on where EXEC loads the program; every CALL FAR with a known target therefore produces one relocation entry. LLIBCE.LIB is compiled in the large model, so its internal calls are far too. Section 5.3 explains the instructions.

Questions.

  1. main calls _sum with push cs followed by a near call. Why is that correct here, and when would the compiler have to emit a real CALL FAR?
  2. Where do the 66 extra relocations of MODL.EXE come from? Use mzdump.py --all and a map made with LINK /MAP.
  3. Before compiling, predict what /AM (medium) and /AC (compact) change in _sum and main. Then check.

Lab 5.3: Inside an OMF object file#

Goal. Find the definitions, references and fixups of HELLO.OBJ, and see the library through the same tool.

What you need. HELLO.OBJ and HELLO.MAP from Lab 5.1, labs/05-toolchain/omfdump.py.

Steps.

  1. python labs/05-toolchain/omfdump.py work/05/HELLO.OBJ --bytes
  2. Find the PUBDEF for _main, the EXTDEF for _printf, and the fixup for the call _printf in main. Match each fixup offset with an instruction in HELLO.COD.
  3. Dump the start-up module of the C library: python labs/05-toolchain/omfdump.py build/dos4/SRC/TOOLS/BLD/LIB/SLIBCE.LIB --member "dos\crt0.asm".
  4. Compile once more with CL /c /Zl /FoHELLOZ.OBJ HELLO.C, dump HELLOZ.OBJ, and try LINK HELLOZ;.

What you should see. Step 1 prints Output 5.11 with the bytes of each LEDATA record:

Output 5.31 – Lab 5.3, the code of HELLO.OBJ (real output; the fixups follow as in Output 5.11)
000144  A0 LEDATA  _TEXT:0000, 48 bytes
                    0000: 55 8b ec 33 c0 e8 00 00 8b 46 04 f7 e8 5d c3 90
                    0010: 33 c0 e8 00 00 ff 36 00 00 e8 e4 ff 83 c4 02 a3
                    0020: 06 00 50 b8 02 00 50 e8 00 00 83 c4 04 2b c0 c3

Step 3 prints Output 5.14. Step 4 shows that /Zl removed the COMENT records for the translator and the default library, and LINK, which no longer knows about SLIBCE.LIB, fails:

Output 5.32 – Lab 5.3, step 4 (real output)
---- LINK HELLOZ;

Microsoft (R) Overlay Linker  Version 3.65
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1983-1988.  All rights reserved.

LINK : warning L4021: no stack segment

LINK : error L2029: Unresolved externals:

__chkstk in file(s):
 HELLOZ.OBJ(HELLO.C)
__acrtused in file(s):
 HELLOZ.OBJ(HELLO.C)
_printf in file(s):
 HELLOZ.OBJ(HELLO.C)

There were 3 errors detected

What is going on. Every zero in the LEDATA bytes that is not a real zero is covered by a fixup, and every fixup offset falls inside an instruction of the .COD listing (the .COD offsets and the LEDATA offsets are the same). Without the default-library comment no library is searched, so the three external names stay undefined, and without crt0 there is not even a stack segment.

Questions.

  1. The fixup at +024 has target _DATA and frame DGROUP. Using HELLO.MAP, compute the 16-bit value LINK writes there, and confirm it in HELLO.EXE (the _TEXT bytes start at file offset 200h + 10h).
  2. Why does the call to _square at offset 19h need no fixup while the call to _printf at 27h does?
  3. Why does LINK warn "no stack segment" only in step 4?

Lab 5.4: MZ headers, relocations and EXE2BIN#

Goal. Read real .EXE headers, make a .COM file, and test the rules of EXE2BIN and EXEC on the real MS-DOS 4.00.

What you need. HELLO.EXE from Lab 5.1, HELLOC.ASM, SEGREF.ASM, BIGCOM.ASM and mkbig.py from labs/05-toolchain, mzdump.py, nasm.

Steps.

  1. Dump three headers: python labs/05-toolchain/mzdump.py work/05/HELLO.EXE, then the same for build/dos4/SRC/CMD/SORT/SORT.EXE and build/dos4/SRC/CMD/FIND/FIND.EXE.

  3. Convert with MS-DOS 4.00's own EXE2BIN, on MS-DOS 4.00:

What you should see. Step 1: Output 5.20 for HELLO.EXE; for SORT.EXE the note "the file ends 11 bytes before the end the header describes"; for FIND.EXE no relocations and the EXEPACK note. Step 2: MASM reports 0 errors and LINK warns L4021: no stack segment for both programs, as it does in the MS-DOS build for every future .COM (Module 0, section 0.3). Steps 3 and 4:

What is going on. HELLOC.EXE satisfies every rule of Listing 5.7: no stack, CS:IP = 0000:0100, no relocations. SEGREF.EXE has IP = 100h too, but MOV AX,SEG MSG needs the segment of MSG, a relocation, so the "Must have no fixups" test rejects it. HELLO.EXE fails the first test, because crt0 brings a stack segment. BIG2.COM is rejected by EXEC itself, before a single instruction runs: the read of FF00h bytes returned FF00h bytes (Listing 5.6), EXEC returned error 8, and COMMAND.COM turned error 8 into message 227 (COMMAND1.ASM lines 426-428), although more than 500 KB of memory was free.

Questions.

  1. HELLOC.EXE is 821 bytes and HELLOC.COM 53. Account for each of the 768 bytes of difference.
  2. Which instruction of E2BINIT.ASM rejects SEGREF.EXE, and which one rejects HELLO.EXE?
  3. Why is the limit 65,279 bytes and not 65,536 or 65,280? What in EXEC.ASM would have to change to allow 65,280?

Lab 5.5: A static library with LIB#

Goal. Build a library, link with it, and see that the linker takes only what is needed.

What you need. ADDUP.C, TIMES.C, USELIB.C from labs/05-toolchain.

Steps.

  1. Compile the three files, try to link the program alone, build MYLIB.LIB, list it, and link again with the library and a map:

    Terminal
    $ python tools/dos_tools.py --dir work/05 "CL /c ADDUP.C TIMES.C USELIB.C" "LINK USELIB;" "LIB MYLIB +ADDUP +TIMES;" "LIB MYLIB,MYLIB.LST;" "TYPE MYLIB.LST" "LINK /MAP USELIB,,,MYLIB;"

  2. Look for _addup and _times in USELIB.MAP, and run python labs/05-toolchain/omfdump.py work/05/MYLIB.LIB --modules.

  3. Run USELIB.EXE on MS-DOS 4.00 with dos_run.py.

What you should see.

Output 5.35 – Lab 5.5, step 1 (real output, abridged)
---- LINK USELIB;
...
LINK : error L2029: Unresolved externals:

_addup in file(s):
 USELIB.OBJ(USELIB.C)

There was 1 error detected
---- LIB MYLIB +ADDUP +TIMES;

Microsoft (R) Library Manager  Version 3.10
Copyright (C) Microsoft Corp 1983-1988.  All rights reserved.

---- TYPE MYLIB.LST
_addup............ADDUP             _times............TIMES


ADDUP             Offset: 00000010H  Code and data size: 10H
  _addup

TIMES             Offset: 00000130H  Code and data size: 10H
  _times
---- LINK /MAP USELIB,,,MYLIB;
...

USELIB.MAP contains 0000:0032 _addup and no _times; omfdump.py --modules lists the two members at the offsets LIB reports (10h and 130h, with a page size of 16 bytes); the program prints 2 + 3 = 5 on MS-DOS 4.00.

What is going on. The first LINK has no library that defines _addup; SLIBCE.LIB is searched (the printf call links) but does not define it. With MYLIB.LIB named on the command line, LINK looks _addup up in the library's dictionary and adds the member ADDUP. Nothing refers to _times, so TIMES stays in the library.

Questions.

  1. Add a call to times(2, 3) to USELIB.C. Predict the new map entries, then check.
  2. Link USELIB.OBJ with ADDUP.OBJ and with a second object that also defines addup. What does LINK say, and why is there no such error when one definition is in an object file and the other in a library?
  3. Build the same library on FreeBSD. Copy ADDUP.C, TIMES.C and USELIB.C to the VM under lower-case names (addup.c, …): clang compiles a file ending in .C as C++. Then run cc -c addup.c times.c && ar rcs libmylib.a addup.o times.o and link with cc -o uselib uselib.c -L. -lmylib. Use nm on the result to show that times is absent.

Lab 5.6: ELF relocatable objects#

Goal. Read sections, symbols and relocations of an ELF object, yours and FreeBSD's.

What you need. labs/05-toolchain/freebsd/bump.asm (Example 5.3), nasm, GNU binutils, build/freebsd/root/usr/lib/crt1.o.

Steps.

  1. nasm -f elf64 -o bump.o bump.asm (in a copy of the freebsd directory).
  2. readelf -h -S bump.o, then readelf -s -r bump.o and objdump -d -r bump.o (Output 5.12).
  3. readelf -s -r build/freebsd/root/usr/lib/crt1.o and objdump -d -r on the same file (Output 5.18).
  4. Put the symbol tables next to the PUBDEF and EXTDEF records of HELLO.OBJ (Output 5.11).

What you should see.

Output 5.36 – Lab 5.6, step 2: header and sections of bump.o (real output, abridged)
  OS/ABI:                            UNIX - System V
  Type:                              REL (Relocatable file)
  Machine:                           Advanced Micro Devices X86-64
There are 7 section headers, starting at offset 0x40:

Section Headers:
  [Nr] Name              Type            Address          Off    Size   ES Flg Lk Inf Al
  [ 0]                   NULL            0000000000000000 000000 000000 00      0   0  0
  [ 1] .data             PROGBITS        0000000000000000 000200 000004 00  WA  0   0  4
  [ 2] .text             PROGBITS        0000000000000000 000210 000019 00  AX  0   0 16
  [ 3] .shstrtab         STRTAB          0000000000000000 000230 000032 00      0   0  1
  [ 4] .symtab           SYMTAB          0000000000000000 000270 0000c0 18      5   4  8
  [ 5] .strtab           STRTAB          0000000000000000 000330 000043 00      0   0  1
  [ 6] .rela.text        RELA            0000000000000000 000380 000060 18      4   2  8
Output 5.37 – Lab 5.6, step 3: the symbols and code relocations of FreeBSD's crt1.o (real file, abridged)
    18: 0000000000000000    37 FUNC    GLOBAL DEFAULT    1 _start
    19: 0000000000000000     0 NOTYPE  GLOBAL DEFAULT  UND main
    20: 0000000000000000     0 NOTYPE  GLOBAL DEFAULT  UND __libc_start1
    21: 0000000000000000     8 OBJECT  GLOBAL DEFAULT   16 __progname
    22: 0000000000000000     8 OBJECT  GLOBAL DEFAULT   18 environ

Relocation section '.rela.text' at offset 0xf8 contains 2 entries:
    Offset             Info             Type               Symbol's Value  Symbol's Name + Addend
0000000000000017  0000001300000001 R_X86_64_64            0000000000000000 main + 0
0000000000000020  0000001400000004 R_X86_64_PLT32         0000000000000000 __libc_start1 - 4

What is going on. .rela.text applies to section 2 (Inf = 2) and uses symbol table 4 (Lk = 4). NASM gives its object the OS/ABI "System V" (0); FreeBSD's objects carry the FreeBSD brand. crt1.o was made by clang, which records types and sizes (FUNC, 37 bytes); NASM records them only if asked. Both files have the same structure as HELLO.OBJ: definitions (PUBDEF / defined symbols), references (EXTDEF / UND) and patches (FIXUPP / .rela).

Questions.

  1. If the linker places bump at 0x401000 and counter at 0x403010, what 4 bytes does it write at offset 2 of bump? Show the calculation S + A - P.
  2. Change global bump to global bump:function and reassemble. What changes in readelf -s?
  3. crt1.o needs an absolute 64-bit address of main. Why is that a problem in a PIE, and how does the PIC branch of Listing 5.2 avoid it?

Lab 5.7: ELF executables and shared libraries#

Goal. Read FreeBSD 15.1's program headers and dynamic sections, and follow a call into a shared library.

What you need. build/freebsd/root (or / in the FreeBSD VM), GNU binutils.

Steps.

  1. readelf -h -l bin/ls (Output 5.22) and readelf -h -l sbin/init (Output 5.23).
  2. readelf -d bin/ls, readelf -d lib/libc.so.7, readelf -d lib/libsys.so.7 (Output 5.26).
  3. readelf -h -l libexec/ld-elf.so.1 and readelf -d libexec/ld-elf.so.1 | grep -E 'NEEDED|SONAME'.
  4. readelf --dyn-syms -W lib/libc.so.7 | grep -w -E 'printf|write|getenv', and the same on lib/libsys.so.7 with __sys_write.
  5. objdump -d bin/ls | grep '@plt>' | head, objdump -d -j .plt bin/ls | head -20 and objdump -s -j .got.plt bin/ls (Output 5.28).
  6. readelf -r bin/ls | grep -c JUMP_SLOT.

What you should see.

Output 5.38 – Lab 5.7, step 3: the run-time linker itself (real file, abridged)
  Type:                              DYN (Shared object file)
  Entry point address:               0x6b70
  LOAD           0x000000 0x0000000000000000 0x0000000000000000 0x005b64 0x005b64 R   0x1000
  LOAD           0x005b70 0x0000000000006b70 0x0000000000006b70 0x0165f1 0x0165f1 R E 0x1000
  LOAD           0x01c170 0x000000000001e170 0x000000000001e170 0x000918 0x000e90 RW  0x1000
  LOAD           0x01ca90 0x000000000001fa90 0x000000000001fa90 0x0003d0 0x0011f8 RW  0x1000
  DYNAMIC        0x01c998 0x000000000001e998 0x000000000001e998 0x0000f0 0x0000f0 RW  0x8

The grep in step 3 prints nothing: ld-elf.so.1 has no INTERP, no NEEDED and no SONAME. Step 4 finds printf and write in libc and __sys_write in libsys (Output 5.27); getenv is in libc as well. Step 6 prints 76.

In the FreeBSD VM the same steps, run in /, give the same numbers (76 JUMP_SLOT entries, the same offsets and flags), but the tools are not GNU binutils. FreeBSD 15.1 builds LLVM's binary utilities by default (the option LLVM_BINUTILS is in the list of options that default to yes, src.opts.mk line 59 and line 127), so readelf, objdump and nm are llvm-readelf, llvm-objdump and llvm-nm under their usual names. The layout differs in small ways, which matters when a script parses it (Exercise 5.6):

Output 5.39 – Lab 5.7, steps 1 and 5 in the course VM with FreeBSD's own tools (captured, abridged)
$ readelf -h -l bin/ls
[...]
  Type:                              DYN (Shared object file)
  Machine:                           Advanced Micro Devices X86-64
  Version:                           0x1
  Entry point address:               0x3AE0
[...]
Program Headers:
  Type           Offset   VirtAddr           PhysAddr           FileSiz  MemSiz   Flg Align
[...]
  LOAD           0x007c60 0x000000000000ac60 0x000000000000ac60 0x0002c0 0x0004d1 RW  0x1000
[...]
 Section to Segment mapping:
  Segment Sections...
[...]
   None   .comment .gnu_debuglink .shstrtab
$ objdump -d -j .plt bin/ls | head -20
[...]
00000000000084f0 <.plt>:
    84f0: ff 35 ba 27 00 00             pushq   0x27ba(%rip)            # 0xacb0
    84f6: ff 25 bc 27 00 00             jmpq    *0x27bc(%rip)           # 0xacb8
    84fc: 0f 1f 40 00                   nopl    (%rax)

0000000000008500 <__libc_start1@plt>:
    8500: ff 25 ba 27 00 00             jmpq    *0x27ba(%rip)           # 0xacc0
    8506: 68 00 00 00 00                pushq   $0x0
    850b: e9 e0 ff ff ff                jmp     0x84f0 <.plt>
[...]
$ ls -li /usr/bin/objdump /usr/bin/llvm-objdump /usr/bin/readelf /usr/bin/llvm-readelf
2020 -r-xr-xr-x  2 root wheel  860208 Jun 12 10:29 /usr/bin/llvm-objdump
2022 -r-xr-xr-x  3 root wheel 1868928 Jun 12 10:29 /usr/bin/llvm-readelf
2020 -r-xr-xr-x  2 root wheel  860208 Jun 12 10:29 /usr/bin/objdump
2022 -r-xr-xr-x  3 root wheel 1868928 Jun 12 10:29 /usr/bin/readelf

The same inode numbers show that objdump and llvm-objdump are one file with two names (a hard link), and so are readelf and llvm-readelf. Compared with GNU readelf (Output 5.22), LLVM's calls a PIE a DYN (Shared object file), prints the entry point in upper case and each program header on one line; llvm-objdump names the first PLT entry <.plt> and writes pushq/jmpq where GNU objdump writes push/jmp. The bytes and addresses are identical.

What is going on. The kernel needs only the program headers: LOAD to map, INTERP to find the run-time linker. The run-time linker needs only DYNAMIC: from it, it finds the NEEDED names, the dynamic symbol table and the relocations. The run-time linker cannot depend on another shared library, because nothing would load that library for it. Its own dynamic section has no NEEDED and no SONAME, but 291 R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations (RELACOUNT 291), which it applies to itself first (section 5.8).

Questions.

  1. The last LOAD segment of ls has FileSiz 0x2c0 and MemSiz 0x4d1. What does the kernel do with the difference, and what is the MS-DOS equivalent in an MZ header?
  2. Which LOAD segment contains .got.plt, and why must it be writable while .plt is not?
  3. /sbin/init is 1,256,544 bytes, /bin/ls 34,992. Explain the difference, and say what ls costs at run time that init does not.

Lab 5.8: The FreeBSD toolchain at work (FreeBSD VM)#

Goal. Run every stage of the FreeBSD pipeline, watch the run-time linker, and compare static and dynamic linking. This lab needs the FreeBSD 15.1 VM. The outputs below were captured in the course VM (15.1-RELEASE, /usr/src at the pinned commit); addresses, inode numbers and dates will differ on yours.

What you need. The FreeBSD VM with nasm (Module 0), a copy of labs/05-toolchain/freebsd.

Steps.

  1. cc -v and cc -### -c hello.c, then cc -### hello.o -o hello.
  2. make hello.i hello.s hello.o and look at each file; make builds the rest (see the Makefile).
  3. ./hello, ls -l hello hello-static, readelf -l hello | grep -A1 INTERP, readelf -l hello-static | grep INTERP.
  4. ldd hello, then LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS=1 ./hello.
  5. LD_BIND_NOW=1 ./hello, then truss ./hello and truss ./hello-static (truss writes to standard error; the program's own output appears among its lines).
  6. ./bumper, and readelf -r bumper | grep -E 'report|counter'.

What you should see.

Output 5.40 – Lab 5.8, step 1 (captured in the course VM; the long command lines are wrapped at argument boundaries, and the -cc1 line is abridged)
$ cc -v
FreeBSD clang version 19.1.7 (https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project.git llvmorg-19.1.7-0-gcd708029e0b2)
Target: x86_64-unknown-freebsd15.1
Thread model: posix
InstalledDir: /usr/bin
$ cc -### -c hello.c
[...]

 "/usr/bin/cc" "-cc1" "-triple" "x86_64-unknown-freebsd15.1" "-emit-obj" [...]
   "-main-file-name" "hello.c" "-mrelocation-model" "static" "-mframe-pointer=all" [...]
   "-internal-externc-isystem" "/usr/include" [...] "-o" "hello.o" "-x" "c" "hello.c"
$ cc -### hello.o -o hello
[...]
 "/usr/bin/ld" "--eh-frame-hdr" "-dynamic-linker" "/libexec/ld-elf.so.1" "--hash-style=both"
   "--enable-new-dtags" "-o" "hello" "/usr/lib/crt1.o" "/usr/lib/crti.o" "/usr/lib/crtbegin.o"
   "-L/usr/lib" "hello.o" "-lgcc" "--as-needed" "-lgcc_s" "--no-as-needed" "-lc" "-lgcc"
   "--as-needed" "-lgcc_s" "--no-as-needed" "/usr/lib/crtend.o" "/usr/lib/crtn.o"

-### prints the commands instead of running them. Compiling is one -cc1 command that -emit-objs directly: there is no separate assembler, and (in-process) says that the driver does not even start a new process for it, it calls the compiler as a function. Linking is one ld command (/usr/bin/ld is a symbolic link to ld.lld). It names /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 as the program interpreter and adds crt1.o, crtbegin.o and crtend.o, not Scrt1.o, crtbeginS.o and crtendS.o, and the compiler was given -mrelocation-model static: cc does not build a PIE unless asked. cc -### -pie hello.o shows -pie, Scrt1.o, crtbeginS.o and crtendS.o, and cc -### -fPIE -c hello.c shows -mrelocation-model pic -pic-level 2 -pic-is-pie. The release's own programs are PIEs only because the base system's makefiles add both flags (section 5.3).

Step 2 writes hello.i (526 lines, starting with # 1 "hello.c" line markers where MS C writes #line) and hello.s, compiled with -O2 by the Makefile:

Output 5.41 – Lab 5.8, step 2: main in hello.s (captured in the course VM, abridged)
main:                                   # @main
        .cfi_startproc
# %bb.0:
        pushq   %rbp
[...]
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
        .cfi_def_cfa_register %rbp
        movl    counter(%rip), %esi
        imull   %esi, %esi
        movl    %esi, table+12(%rip)
        movl    $.L.str, %edi
        xorl    %eax, %eax
        callq   printf
        xorl    %eax, %eax
        popq    %rbp
[...]
        .type   table,@object                   # @table
        .bss
        .globl  table
        .p2align        4, 0x0
table:
        .zero   400

Compare it with MS C's Output 5.5: square is inlined (one imull), table[3] is table+12 because an int has 4 bytes, the arguments of printf travel in %edi and %esi, and %al = 0 (the first xorl %eax, %eax) tells a variadic function that no vector registers carry arguments. movl $.L.str, %edi loads the string's address as a 32-bit constant: allowed only because the program is not position-independent and will be linked below 4 GB. table is an ordinary symbol in .bss, not a communal variable like MS C's COMM (Output 5.6).

Output 5.42 – Lab 5.8, step 3 (captured in the course VM)
$ ./hello
hello, world: 49
$ ls -l hello hello-static
-rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel    9832 Nov  9 09:53 hello
-rwxr-xr-x  1 root wheel 4402664 Nov  9 09:53 hello-static
$ readelf -l hello | grep -A1 INTERP
  INTERP         0x0002a8 0x00000000002002a8 0x00000000002002a8 0x000015 0x000015 R   0x1
      [Requesting program interpreter: /libexec/ld-elf.so.1]
$ readelf -l hello-static | grep INTERP

hello asks for the run-time linker, and its INTERP header sits at 0x2002a8, not near 0 as in ls (Output 5.22): an EXEC file linked at 0x200000. hello-static has no INTERP (the last grep prints nothing and exits with status 1) and is about 450 times larger, and three and a half times the size of /sbin/init (Output 5.23), which contains more code. The difference is debugging information: the members of /usr/lib/libc.a carry compressed DWARF sections (readelf -S shows them with flag C), the linker writes them out uncompressed, and in hello-static the .debug_* sections take about 3.5 MB. strip leaves 709,024 bytes (3,992 for hello); the release's programs are installed stripped, with a .gnu_debuglink section pointing to a separate debug file (Output 5.39 lists it for ls).

Output 5.43 – Lab 5.8, step 4 (captured in the course VM; addresses change from run to run)
$ ldd hello
hello:
        libc.so.7 => /lib/libc.so.7 (0x3bbba13ae000)
        libsys.so.7 => /lib/libsys.so.7 (0x3bbba1b28000)
        [vdso] (0x3bbba06cc000)
$ LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS=1 ./hello

        libsys.so.7 => /lib/libsys.so.7 (0x821fd1000)
        [vdso] (0x820597000)
$ LD_BIND_NOW=1 ./hello
hello, world: 49

The lines follow the formats in rtld.c line 5215 and line 5317. LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS=1 ./hello prints the same list without the hello: line, which ldd prints itself (ldd.c line 210), and hello does not run. The addresses are in a different range because ldd does not exec the program: it runs /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 -- hello (ldd.c lines 238-240), so the kernel starts the run-time linker, an ET_DYN file, as the program and places it at a random high address, and the run-time linker maps hello and the libraries itself. For ./hello, an EXEC file at 0x200000, the libraries land lower; a PIE (cc -fPIE -pie) gets high addresses too. LD_BIND_NOW changes nothing visible: printf is bound before main instead of at its first call.

Everything before fstat(1, ...) in the first listing happens before main: the run-time linker at work, in the order of section 5.8. issetugid decides whether the LD_ variables may be trusted (rtld.c line 593). /etc/libmap.conf and the hints file ld-elf.so.hints, with its search path /lib:/usr/lib:..., come from the search rules of section 5.7. Each library is then mapped in four moves: one page to read the ELF and program headers (map_object.c line 404), a MAP_GUARD reservation of the whole address range, one MAP_FIXED mapping per PT_LOAD segment (read-only, read-execute at file offset 0x93000, read-write) and an anonymous mapping for the BSS (map_object.c lines 196-285). libsys.so.7 is opened right after libc, as libc's NEEDED entry. The mprotect(...,PROT_READ) calls make each GNU_RELRO area read-only after relocation, sysarch(AMD64_SET_TLSBASE) installs thread-local storage, and readlink("/etc/malloc.conf") is libc's memory allocator initializing itself. The last mprotect, at 0x202000, is hello's own GNU_RELRO page, made read-only just before the jump to _start (rtld.c lines 1030-1032). In all, truss prints 55 lines for one write, against 12 for the static program, which opens and maps no file: its first system call is the allocator's readlink, made by libc code that the linker copied into hello-static.

Relocation section '.rela.plt' at offset 0x460 contains 2 entries:
    Offset             Info             Type               Symbol's Value  Symbol's Name + Addend
00000000002038b8  0000000100000007 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT     0000000000000000 __libc_start1@FBSD_1.7 + 0
00000000002038c0  0000000200000007 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT     0000000000000000 printf@FBSD_1.0 + 0
$ objdump -d bumper | grep -A6 "<bump>:"
0000000000201690 <bump>:
  201690: 8b 05 02 22 00 00             movl    0x2202(%rip), %eax      # 0x203898 <counter>
  201696: 03 05 00 22 00 00             addl    0x2200(%rip), %eax      # 0x20389c <step>
  20169c: 89 05 f6 21 00 00             movl    %eax, 0x21f6(%rip)      # 0x203898 <counter>
  2016a2: 89 c7                         movl    %eax, %edi
  2016a4: e9 87 ff ff ff                jmp     0x201630 <report>
  2016a9: cc                            int3

The grep prints nothing: no relocation for report or counter is left. ld.lld placed bump, report and counter in the same EXEC file at fixed addresses, so it applied all four relocations of Output 5.12 itself. The PLT32 relocation for report became a direct jmp (e9 87 ff ff ff, back to 0x201630), with no PLT entry, because report is not in a shared library. Only the two calls into libc.so.7 remain for the run-time linker, as JUMP_SLOT entries.

What is going on. cc is a driver like CL (section 5.2): it runs the compiler with an integrated assembler and then ld.lld with the start-up files of section 5.5. ldd and LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS use the run-time linker's own loading code (Listing 5.17), so they show exactly what will be loaded.

Questions.

  1. Compare the cc -### link command with LINK's response file (Output 5.3). Which file plays the role of crt0, and how does each linker learn the name of the C library?
  2. Why does ldd list libsys.so.7 although hello does not need it directly?
  3. Compare the sizes of hello, hello-static and HELLO.EXE. What does each one contain?

Study cases#

Study case 5.A: One printf, two systems#

printf("hello, world: %d\n", table[3]) is one line in both HELLO.C and hello.c. Here is everything that runs between that line and the bytes leaving the process, with the file each piece lives in.

MS-DOS 4.00. Everything up to the INT 21h instruction is inside HELLO.EXE; LINK copied it from SLIBCE.LIB (Output 5.13 lists each routine's address):

  1. _main pushes the two arguments and calls _printf (Output 5.5).
  2. _printf (printf.c, 60 bytes) gives stdout a temporary buffer with __stbuf, formats with __output (output.c, 2,267 bytes, the largest member HELLO uses), and flushes the temporary buffer with __ftbuf. These names are its EXTDEFs.
  3. __ftbuf (_sftbuf.c) calls _fflush (fflush.c), whose EXTDEF list contains _write.
  4. _write (write.asm) executes MOV AH,40h and INT 21h with the handle in BX.
  5. INT 21h enters MSDOS.SYS through the interrupt vector table: the dispatcher, the handle and System File Table lookup, and a call to the device driver (Module 2, sections 2.2 and 2.3, and Study case 2.A, which follows a read the same way). For the screen the driver is CON in IO.SYS, whose character output ends in the BIOS teletype function, INT 10h with AH=0Eh (MSBIO1.ASM lines 584-594). (Under dos_run.py the output is redirected to COM1, so the serial driver is used instead.)

FreeBSD 15.1. Only main is in hello; everything else is in shared libraries that the run-time linker attached:

  1. main calls printf through its PLT entry; on the first call _rtld_bind fills the GOT slot (Listing 5.14).
  2. printf (libc) calls vfprintf, the formatter; stdio buffers the text and eventually calls __swrite, which calls _write(fp->_file, buf, n) (stdio.c lines 57-61).
  3. _write is found in libsys through libc's auxiliary filter (section 5.7): it is the 17-byte stub __sys_write (Output 5.27), which loads system call number 4 and executes syscall.
  4. The kernel's sys_write (Module 2, section 2.2.5) writes to the terminal through the file and the tty layer.
MS-DOS 4.00 FreeBSD 15.1
Code that formats the number __output, copied into HELLO.EXE vfprintf, in /lib/libc.so.7
How the library is reached near CALL within _TEXT CALL to the PLT, JMP through the GOT
Last instruction in user code INT 21h (AH=40h) syscall (%eax = 4)
Program file HELLO.EXE, 7,271 bytes, self-contained hello, 9,832 bytes (Output 5.42; 3,992 stripped), plus libc.so.7 (2,075,224 bytes), libsys.so.7 (111,392) and ld-elf.so.1 (120,400), shared with every process
Kernel MSDOS.SYS 37,376 bytes + IO.SYS 33,321 the FreeBSD kernel (Module 1)

Nothing in the MS-DOS column is shared at run time except MSDOS.SYS and IO.SYS. Ten C programs on a floppy carry ten copies of __output; at least they never run at the same time. On FreeBSD a few hundred programs and their processes share one copy of vfprintf on disk and, because the code pages are mapped from the same file, in memory.

Discussion questions:

  1. Which steps of each column run with a different privilege level from main, and which could a debugger single-step through?
  2. A bug in the number formatting is fixed in a new C library. What has to happen on each system before HELLO prints correctly?

Study case 5.B: Relocation twice#

Both systems link programs for an address that is not where they will run, and both leave a list of the places to correct. SEGS.C (labs/05-toolchain/SEGS.C) prints where EXEC put its segments:

Output 5.46 – SEGS.EXE on MS-DOS 4.00 (real output; SEGS.MAP gives DGROUP = 0173:0 and _counter = 0173:007C)
---- SEGS
PSP 1204  CS 1214  DS 1387  SS 1387  &counter 1387:007C

EXEC allocated a block, built the PSP at segment 1204h and loaded the image right after it, at 1214h: that is exec_rel_fac. mzdump.py SEGS.EXE lists four relocations, each pointing at a word that holds 0173h. EXEC added 1214h to each (Listing 5.9), so crt0's mov di,0173h became mov di,1387h, and DS = SS = 1387h is DGROUP's real place: 1214h + 173h. &counter is 1387:007C, the map's offset unchanged. Only segment values are relocated; offsets never change, because the image is moved in whole paragraphs and every offset is relative to a segment register. The segment numbers depend on what was in memory before the program was loaded; the offsets do not.

On FreeBSD, ls is linked at address 0 and has 16 relocations in .rela.dyn and 76 in .rela.plt (Output 5.26, Lab 5.7). Its first relocation reads:

Output 5.47 – the first entries of readelf -r bin/ls (real file)
Relocation section '.rela.dyn' at offset 0x1350 contains 16 entries:
    Offset             Info             Type               Symbol's Value  Symbol's Name + Addend
00000000000099e0  0000000000000008 R_X86_64_RELATIVE                         1d78
...
0000000000009c20  0000001d00000006 R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT      0000000000000000 __stdoutp@FBSD_1.0 + 0

With a base address B chosen by the kernel, ld-elf.so.1 writes B + 0x1d78 into the 8 bytes at B + 0x99e0 (reloc.c lines 310-312): the same "add the load address" as EXEC's ADD [BX],SI, but with byte addresses instead of paragraph numbers. The GLOB_DAT entry is something MS-DOS never needed: the address of __stdoutp, a variable in another file, libc.so.7, found by name at run time.

MZ .EXE on MS-DOS 4.00 PIE on FreeBSD 15.1
Linked for segment 0 address 0
What moves the whole image, in paragraphs each object, in pages, to a base chosen by the kernel (random with ASLR)
Relocation entry 4 bytes: seg:off of a word 24 bytes: r_offset, r_info (symbol, type), r_addend
Kinds one: add the load segment RELATIVE, GLOB_DAT, JUMP_SLOT, TPOFF64, …
Applied by the kernel (EXEC), before the program starts the run-time linker, in the process; PLT slots lazily
Pages touched any word in the image data pages only (GOT, .data.rel.ro); code stays shared and read-only
Afterwards the image is ordinary memory GNU_RELRO made read-only
HELLO / ls 4 entries 16 + 76 entries

The last two rows explain why ELF goes to the trouble of a GOT. If the dynamic linker patched addresses in the code, as EXEC does, every process would need its own copy of the code pages. By keeping all addresses in a table in the data segment, the code of libc.so.7 is identical in every process and can be shared.

Discussion questions:

  1. Why may a .COM file contain no relocations, and how do CONVERT's stub (section 5.6) and LINK's /EXEPACK unpacker get around that rule?
  2. What would it cost FreeBSD to relocate code the way EXEC does, by patching instructions in place?

Study case 5.C: Why MS-DOS never had shared libraries#

Shared libraries need three things that MS-DOS 4.00 did not have or did not need.

  1. A reason. Sharing saves memory when several programs run at once. MS-DOS runs one program at a time (plus resident programs that borrow the CPU, Module 2, section 2.2.4); two copies of printf are never in memory together unless one program EXECs another.
  2. A loader that knows names. EXEC relocates segment numbers and nothing else; there is no symbol table in the .EXE, no list of needed files, no search path. FreeBSD's loader for names, ld-elf.so.1, is 120,400 bytes, more than MSDOS.SYS and IO.SYS together.
  3. Cheap calls into another image. In the small model a call into a separately loaded library would need a CALL FAR, and in the small and medium models (whose calls are already far) far data pointers, the costs measured in Lab 5.2.

What MS-DOS used instead was the interrupt vector table: a call by number through a pointer that the provider installs. The operating system itself is the main shared library: every program reaches MSDOS.SYS's file system, memory manager and EXEC through INT 21h. Resident programs and installable drivers extend it the same way: they stay in memory (INT 21h function 31h, $Keep_process, Module 2), hook a vector, and any program can call them. Since vectors are few, MS-DOS shares one of them, INT 2Fh, the multiplex interrupt: a program puts a channel number in AH and each resident handler checks whether the call is for it. The MS-DOS 4.00 source keeps the registry of channels:

MS-DOS 4.00Listing 5.18 – The registry of INT 2Fh channels (MULT.INC lines 24-52)Source ↗
; The current set of defined multiplex channels is (* means documented):
;
;   Channel(h)  Issuer          Receiver    Function
;      00       server          PSPRINT     print job control
;     *01       print/apps      PRINT       Queueing of files
;      02       BIOS            REDIR       signal open/close of printers
;
;      05       command         REDIR       obtain text of net int 24 message
;     *06       server/assign   ASSIGN      Install check
;
;      08       external driver IBMBIO      interface to internal routines
;
;      10       sharer/server   Sharer      install check
;      11       DOS/server      Redir       install check/redirection funcs
;      12       sharer/redir    DOS         dos functions and structure maint
;      13       MSNET           MSNET       movement of NCBs
;      13       external driver IBMBIO      Reset_Int_13, allows installation
;                                           of alternative INT_13 drivers after
;                                           boot_up
;      14 (IBM) DOS             NLSFUNC     down load NLS country info,DOS 3.3
;      14 (MS)  APPS            POPUP       MSDOS 4 popup screen functions
;      15       APPS            MSCDEX      CD-ROM extensions interface
;      16       WIN386          WIN386      Windows communications
;      17       Clipboard       WINDOWS     Clipboard interface
;     *18       Applications    MS-Manger   Toggle interface to manager
;      19       Shell
;      1A       Ansi.sys
;      1B       Fastopen,Vdisk   IBMBIO     EMS INT 67H stub handler
;

Read it as a list of shared services: the print spooler, SHARE, the network redirector, national language support, the CD-ROM extensions, Windows. Each channel number is what a SONAME is on FreeBSD, a name agreed in advance; each install check is what dlopen does, asking whether the service is present; and the channel's sub-functions are its exported symbols, numbered instead of named. The MS-DOS kernel itself answers on channel 12h, for SHARE and the redirector. The comment also shows the price of numbers instead of names: channel 13h has two owners, and 14h means one thing on IBM's version and another on Microsoft's.

The other technique of the time was overlays: LINK 3.65 calls itself the "Overlay Linker", and EXEC's function 3 loads code into memory a program already owns (Module 2, section 2.6). Overlays let a large program reuse its own memory for code it needs at different times. They save memory within one program, as shared libraries do across programs, but nothing is shared.

Discussion questions:

  1. Compare an INT 2Fh channel number with a SONAME and with a symbol version such as FBSD_1.7: what conflict does each prevent, and what goes wrong when two parties choose the same one?
  2. Could MS-DOS 4.00 on an 8088 have supported shared libraries? Sketch what EXEC and the .EXE format would have needed, and what it would have cost a program in the small model.

Homework#

Exercise 5.1: One function, two compilers#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 3 h.

Tasks:

  1. Write a C function unsigned checksum(const unsigned char *p, unsigned n) that returns the 16-bit ones' complement sum of n bytes (like CHKSUM in COMMAND2.ASM, Module 3) in a file of its own.
  2. Compile it with MS C 5.10 with /Fc and each of /Od, /Os, /Ot, /Ox, in the small and the large model. Record the code size of _checksum from each .COD listing.
  3. In the FreeBSD VM, compile it with cc -c at -O0, -O1, -O2 and -Os, and record the size of checksum from nm -S on each object file; cc -S with the same options gives the code to read.
  4. Make a table and explain three differences in instruction choice (registers versus stack, loop instructions, unrolling or vectorization, far pointers).

Deliverables: the source, the listings, the table and a one-page explanation.

Hints: nm -S prints symbol sizes. MS C's /Ox includes /Gs, so __chkstk disappears.

Exercise 5.2: The entry point as a file offset#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2 h.

Tasks:

  1. Extend labs/05-toolchain/mzdump.py to print the file offset of the entry point and of the initial stack, and the file offset of each relocated word.
  2. For HELLO.EXE, dump 16 bytes at the entry point with ndisasm -b16 -e <offset> -k ... or a few lines of Python and show that they are the start of __astart (Output 5.15).
  3. For FDISK.EXE, which is packed, print the file offset of the unpacker's entry and of the real entry point recorded in the EXEPACK header, and explain why the second offset is meaningless in the file.

Deliverables: your mzdump.py, its output for HELLO.EXE, SORT.EXE and FDISK.EXE, and your answer to task 3.

Hints: the image starts at e_cparhdr * 16; segment values in the header are relative to the image.

Exercise 5.3: A static library, in C and assembly, on both systems#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 4 h.

Tasks:

  1. Write a library of two modules: reverse (reverse a string in place) in C and upcase (convert a string to upper case) in assembly language. On MS-DOS use MASM 5.10 syntax and the MS C small-model convention (_upcase, argument at [bp+4], preserve SI, DI, BP); on FreeBSD use NASM and the System V convention (argument in %rdi).
  2. Build STR.LIB with LIB and libstr.a with ar, and a test program that uses only upcase.
  3. Show with the map (/MAP) and with nm that reverse was not linked, then change the test program so that it is.
  4. Run the MS-DOS version on MS-DOS 4.00 with dos_run.py and the FreeBSD version in the VM.

Deliverables: sources, build commands, maps and nm output, and the program output on both systems.

Hints: MS C's library already has a function strrev, hence the name reverse. MASM 5.10 converts public names to upper case unless you assemble with /Mx (the MS-DOS build does, TOOLS.INI line 30); LINK on its own ignores case, but CL runs it with /NOI, so _UPCASE does not satisfy _upcase. .MODEL SMALL and .CODE give the right segment names. In NASM, global upcase:function gives the symbol a type.

Exercise 5.4: Two link errors, explained from the object files#

Difficulty: intermediate. Estimated time: 2.5 h.

Tasks:

  1. On MS-DOS, produce L2029: Unresolved externals and L2025: symbol defined more than once (Lab 5.5, question 2). For each, name the OMF records (EXTDEF, PUBDEF) that cause it and show them with omfdump.py.
  2. In the FreeBSD VM, produce the same two errors with cc and record ld.lld's messages. Show the symbol table entries (UND, GLOBAL) responsible, with readelf -s.
  3. FreeBSD can also fail at run time: build a shared library libx.so with a function f, link a program against it, then rebuild libx.so without f. Run the program with and without LD_BIND_NOW=1 and explain the difference with Listing 5.14 and rtld(1).
  4. Explain why MS-DOS has no equivalent of task 3.

Deliverables: transcripts and a one-page explanation.

Hints: cc -shared -fPIC -o libx.so x.c, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. to run the program.

Exercise 5.5: ldd without running the program#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 4 h.

Tasks:

  1. Write needed.py, a Python program that reads an ELF64 file, finds PT_DYNAMIC through the program headers, and prints its NEEDED, SONAME, AUXILIARY and RUNPATH entries (strings come from the dynamic string table, located through DT_STRTAB converted to a file offset with the PT_LOAD headers).
  2. Make it recursive: look the needed names up in lib and usr/lib under a root directory you pass, and print the tree for build/freebsd/root/bin/ls.
  3. Compare the result with ldd /bin/ls in the FreeBSD VM and explain every difference (the vDSO, the order, the filter).
  4. Explain why ldd's approach (running the run-time linker) is more reliable, and why it is also more dangerous for an untrusted file.

Deliverables: needed.py, its output, the comparison and the explanation.

Hints: struct.unpack_from("<qQ", ...) reads one Elf64_Dyn (Output 5.26 shows the tags). DT_STRTAB is a virtual address, not a file offset.

Exercise 5.6: Classifying executables with scripts#

Difficulty: basic. Estimated time: 2.5 h.

Tasks:

  1. FreeBSD: write a sh script elfkind.sh that, for every file in /bin and /sbin, prints static, PIE or exec, and then a count of how many programs need each shared library, sorted by count. Use readelf -h -l -d and standard tools (awk, sort, uniq).
  2. MS-DOS 4.00: write COMKIND.BAT that takes names of .EXE files without extension, runs EXE2BIN on each, and prints NAME: converted or NAME: not convertible depending on whether NAME.COM exists afterwards. Run it with dos_run.py on HELLOC, SEGREF and HELLO from Lab 5.4.
  3. Explain, for the three programs, which rule of Listing 5.7 decided the result.

Deliverables: both scripts and their output.

Hints: SHIFT and IF "%1"=="" loop over arguments; IF EXIST tests for a file. EXE2BIN prints its message to standard output, so >NUL hides it. In the VM readelf is LLVM's (Output 5.39): test your awk and sed patterns on its output, and remember that some names in /sbin are symbolic links.

Exercise 5.7: Essay: what executable formats assume#

Difficulty: advanced. Estimated time: 3 h.

Write 1,200-1,500 words on how the .COM, MZ and ELF formats encode the assumptions of their operating systems: one program or many, one address space or many, segments or pages, a loader in the kernel or in user mode, names resolved before or after loading. For each field of the MZ header and for PT_LOAD, PT_INTERP, PT_DYNAMIC and PT_GNU_RELRO, say which assumption it serves. Support every claim with a permalink or with output from this module's labs.

Deliverables: the essay.

Hints: start from the comparison tables in sections 5.6 and 5.8 and from Study case 5.B.

Further reading#

  • The MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Microsoft Press, 1988: the chapters on .COM and .EXE programs, object modules (OMF records) and the linker.
  • Tool Interface Standard (TIS) Committee, Relocatable Object Module Format (OMF) Specification, version 1.1, 1993: the full record catalogue that omfdump.py implements in part.
  • Tool Interface Standard (TIS) Committee, Executable and Linking Format (ELF) Specification, version 1.2, 1995, and the System V Application Binary Interface, AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement (the x86-64 psABI): relocation types, code models, PLT and GOT.
  • John R. Levine, Linkers and Loaders, Morgan Kaufmann, 2000: object formats (including OMF and ELF), relocation, libraries and dynamic linking, explained across systems.
  • Ulrich Drepper, How To Write Shared Libraries, 2011: what PIC, the PLT and the GOT cost, from the library author's side.
  • FreeBSD manual pages rtld(1), ldd(1), elf(5), ld.lld(1) and ar(1), https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=rtld&sektion=1&manpath=FreeBSD+15.1-RELEASE and neighbours.
  • The sources read in this module: v4.0/src/DOS/EXEC.ASM, v4.0/src/CMD/EXE2BIN, lib/csu, libexec/rtld-elf and sys/kern/imgact_elf.c.
